chapters.heading: 1. Physiographic Divisions of India
chapters.body_markdown:
**Overview:** The six physical regions that make up India — and the geological story behind each.

**Core Mental Model:** India has six physiographic divisions, each born of a different geological process: collision-built mountains, alluvium-built plains, ancient stable plateau, sand desert, sediment-built coasts, and offshore islands of coral and volcano.

### India’s Six Physiographic Divisions

| Division | Geological Origin | Signature Exam Feature |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Northern & NE Mountains | Young fold (Indo-Australian × Eurasian) | ~2,400 km; Himadri, Himachal, Shiwalik |
| Northern Plains | Quaternary river alluvium | Indus–Ganga–Brahmaputra; Bhabar, Terai, Bhangar, Khadar |
| Peninsular Plateau | **Oldest** Gondwana crystalline shield | Deccan Traps, Western & Eastern Ghats |
| Indian Desert (Thar) | Arid aeolian sands | Rain shadow of Aravallis; Luni river |
| Coastal Plains | Marine & river deposition | Narrow West (Konkan, Malabar) vs Wide East (Coromandel) |
| Islands | Coral & volcanic | Lakshadweep (coral) · Andaman & Nicobar (volcanic — Barren Island) |

### High-Yield Exam Facts

- India has six physiographic divisions: Northern & NE Mountains, Northern Plains, Peninsular Plateau, Indian Desert, Coastal Plains, and Islands. The Peninsular Plateau is the oldest; the Himalayas and the Northern Plains are the youngest.
- The Himalayas are young fold mountains, formed by the ongoing collision of the Indo-Australian plate with the Eurasian plate (started about 50 million years ago). They stretch ~2,400 km from the Indus in the west to the Brahmaputra in the east.
- The Himalayas have three parallel ranges, from south to north: Shiwaliks (Outer, 900–1,100 m), Himachal/Lesser (3,500–4,500 m), and Himadri/Greater (>6,000 m, with peaks above 8,000 m). The Trans-Himalayas lie further north and include the Karakoram, Ladakh, and Zaskar ranges.
- The Purvanchal (Eastern Hills) are a southward continuation of the Himalayas after the Dihang gorge. They include the Patkai, Naga, Manipur, and Mizo (Lushai) Hills — the entire chain runs largely north–south.
- Mizoram lies almost entirely within the Mizo Hills, part of the Patkai–Arakan Yoma system. Phawngpui (Blue Mountain), 2,157 m, is the highest peak in Mizoram. About 90% of the state is hilly terrain.
- The Northern Plains were formed by alluvial deposits from the Indus, Ganga, and Brahmaputra systems filling a depression between the rising Himalayas and the old Peninsular block. The plain is ~2,400 km long and 240–320 km wide.
- The Northern Plains are divided into four sub-belts from north to south: Bhabar (8–16 km pebble belt at Shiwalik foot — rivers go underground), Tarai (marshy, very fertile — Corbett & Kaziranga are here), Bhangar (older alluvium with calcareous "kankar" nodules), and Khadar (newer alluvium, flooded yearly, most fertile).
- The Peninsular Plateau is India’s oldest landmass — part of the ancient Gondwana supercontinent. It is geologically stable, rich in minerals, and triangular in shape, bounded by the Aravallis (NW), Vindhya-Satpura (N), Western Ghats (W), and Eastern Ghats (E).
- The Peninsular Plateau has two major sub-regions: the Central Highlands (north of the Narmada — Malwa, Bundelkhand, Chotanagpur plateaus) and the Deccan Plateau (south of the Narmada, the larger half).
- The Thar Desert (Indian Desert) lies west of the Aravallis, mostly in western Rajasthan. It receives less than 250 mm of rain a year, has shifting sand dunes (barchans), and an underground stream system fed by the now-vanished Ghaggar-Hakra (ancient Saraswati) river.
- The Western Coastal Plain is narrow (50–100 km), faces the Arabian Sea, and is divided into Konkan (north), Kanara (middle), and Malabar (south). The Western Ghats rise sharply behind it.
- The Eastern Coastal Plain is wider (100–130 km), faces the Bay of Bengal, and is divided into Northern Circars (north) and Coromandel (south). All major peninsular rivers — Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri — form deltas here.
- The Andaman & Nicobar Islands (Bay of Bengal) are of volcanic/tectonic origin — a southward continuation of the Arakan Yoma. They are separated from each other by the 10° Channel. Saddle Peak (737 m) in North Andaman is their highest point. Barren Island is the only active volcano in India.
- The Lakshadweep Islands (Arabian Sea) are coral atolls formed over volcanic seamounts of the Reunion Hotspot. They include around 36 islands; Kavaratti is the capital. They are flat and low-lying — highly vulnerable to sea-level rise.
- Highest peaks to remember: Kanchenjunga (8,586 m) is the highest peak entirely within India (Sikkim). Anaimudi (2,695 m) is the highest in Peninsular India (Kerala). Guru Shikhar (1,722 m) is the highest in the Aravallis. Phawngpui (2,157 m) is the highest in Mizoram. K2 (8,611 m) lies in PoK — administered by Pakistan, claimed by India.

chapters.heading: 2. Mountains & Passes of India
chapters.body_markdown:
**Overview:** The young Himalayas, the ancient Peninsular ranges, and the strategic passes that connect India to the world.

**Core Mental Model:** India has two kinds of mountains: the young, still-rising Himalayas (and the Purvanchal’s curve into Mizoram) and the ancient, eroded Peninsular ranges. Where these mountains have notches — the passes — trade, pilgrimage, war, and modern strategy converge.

### High-Yield Exam Facts

- India’s mountains divide into two families: the young fold Himalayas in the north (still rising due to ongoing India-Eurasia collision) and the ancient block-mountain ranges of the Peninsula (worn down over hundreds of millions of years).
- The Himalayas have four parallel zones north-to-south: (1) Trans-Himalayas — Karakoram, Ladakh, Zaskar (cold desert, K2 is here); (2) Himadri / Greater Himalayas — highest range, >6,000 m, contains Everest, Kanchenjunga, Nanda Devi; (3) Himachal / Lesser Himalayas — 3,500–4,500 m, hill stations; (4) Shiwaliks / Outer Himalayas — youngest, 900–1,100 m, formed from river sediments.
- The Himalayas run ~2,400 km from the Indus gorge in the west to the Brahmaputra gorge in the east. They are wider in the west (~400 km in Kashmir) and narrower in the east (~150 km in Arunachal). Beyond the Dihang/Brahmaputra gorge, they curve south as the Purvanchal Ranges.
- The Purvanchal is the southward curve of the Himalayan system after the Dihang gorge — Patkai, Naga, Manipur, Mizo (Lushai), Tripura Hills. They run north–south (unlike the Himalayas which run east–west). The Mizo Hills, in which all of Mizoram lies, are part of this system.
- Peninsular ranges (oldest first): The Aravalli (~1.7 billion years old, one of the oldest mountain ranges on Earth) runs NE-SW through Rajasthan; Guru Shikhar (1722 m) is the highest point. The Vindhya and Satpura ranges divide North from South India and frame the Narmada rift valley between them.
- The Western Ghats (Sahyadri) run ~1,600 km along the west coast, with the Arabian Sea on one side and the Deccan Plateau on the other. They are a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the world’s eight "hottest" biodiversity hotspots. Highest peak: Anaimudi (2,695 m) in Kerala — the highest in Peninsular India.
- The Eastern Ghats are NOT continuous — they are broken into discontinuous hill groups by the great east-flowing rivers (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri). They are lower, older, and more eroded than the Western Ghats. Highest peak: Mahendragiri (1,501 m) in Odisha.
- Highest peak quick reference: K2 (8,611 m) — PoK, claimed by India. Kanchenjunga (8,586 m) — highest peak ENTIRELY within India. Nanda Devi (7,816 m) — second-highest entirely in India’s undisputed territory. Anaimudi (2,695 m) — highest in Peninsular India. Phawngpui (2,157 m) — highest in Mizoram and the entire Purvanchal.
- Karakoram Pass (5,540 m, Ladakh) connects India to China’s Xinjiang — part of the ancient Silk Route. Zoji La (3,580 m) is the strategic pass on the Srinagar–Leh highway, closed by snow in winter — a Zoji La tunnel is under construction for all-weather access.
- Rohtang Pass (3,978 m, Himachal Pradesh) connected Manali to Lahaul-Spiti seasonally. Today, the Atal Tunnel (opened 2020, 9.02 km) runs beneath it — once the world’s longest highway tunnel above 10,000 ft — giving all-weather access to Leh.
- Nathu La (4,310 m, Sikkim) was reopened for limited India–China border trade in 2006 after being closed since the 1962 war. Jelep La (next to Nathu La) was the historic route to Lhasa used by the British. Bomdi La and Bum La (Arunachal) lead to Tawang and Tibet.
- Lipulekh Pass (5,334 m, Uttarakhand) is the traditional pilgrim route to Kailash-Mansarovar; the recent road extension to the pass triggered a 2020 border dispute with Nepal. Mana and Niti passes (also Uttarakhand) are old Tibet trade routes.
- Umling La (5,882 m, Ladakh) is the highest motorable pass in the world — constructed by the Border Roads Organisation. Khardung La (5,359 m) leads from Leh to the Nubra Valley and Siachen.
- Western Ghats passes: the Palakkad Gap is the largest breach (~140 km wide) and the main route between Kerala and Tamil Nadu — it shapes monsoon patterns by letting moist air through. Thal Ghat (Mumbai–Nashik) and Bhor Ghat (Mumbai–Pune) carry Maharashtra’s busiest road and rail traffic.
- Mizoram-specific: the Mizo Hills run north–south through the state and continue south into Myanmar’s Chin State as the Arakan Yoma. Phawngpui (Blue Mountain) at 2,157 m is the highest. Several smaller hill ranges — Tlawng Hill, Lurh Tlang, and others — give Mizoram its distinctive ridge-and-valley topography.

chapters.heading: 3. Rivers of India
chapters.body_markdown:
**Overview:** The two great river families of India — and how their origin shapes their character.

**Core Mental Model:** Where a river is born decides what it is. Himalayan rivers (snow-fed, perennial, fertile floodplains) and Peninsular rivers (rain-fed, seasonal, mature stable courses) define almost every geography question about Indian water.

### Himalayan vs. Peninsular Rivers

| Feature | Himalayan Rivers | Peninsular Rivers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Source | Snow + glaciers + rain (perennial) | Rain-fed (mostly seasonal) |
| Examples | Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra | Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, Mahanadi, Narmada, Tapi |
| Flow direction | Mostly East → Bay of Bengal (Indus → Arabian Sea) | East → Bay of Bengal **except Narmada & Tapi** (West → Arabian Sea, rift valleys) |

**Exam Trap:** **Narmada and Tapi** flow *westward* through rift valleys and form **estuaries** (not deltas). **Godavari** is the longest Peninsular river ("Dakshin Ganga").

### High-Yield Exam Facts

- Indian rivers fall into two great families: Himalayan rivers (snow + glacier fed, perennial, long, with wide fertile floodplains) and Peninsular rivers (rain-fed, mostly seasonal, mature, stable courses cut into hard rock). India has 12 major river basins (catchment > 20,000 km²).
- The Indus rises near Lake Mansarovar in Tibet, enters India in Ladakh, then flows into Pakistan to the Arabian Sea. Its five main tributaries — Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Satluj — give the Punjab ("Land of Five Rivers") its name.
- The Indus Waters Treaty (1960), brokered by the World Bank, gives the three eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Satluj) to India and the three western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) primarily to Pakistan. India retains limited rights on the western rivers (run-of-river hydropower, navigation).
- The Ganga begins as the Bhagirathi from the Gangotri Glacier. At Devprayag (Uttarakhand) it joins the Alaknanda and becomes the Ganga. The Ganga basin is the most densely populated river basin on Earth, supporting over 500 million people.
- The Yamuna originates from the Yamunotri Glacier, flows parallel to the Ganga, and joins it at Prayagraj (Allahabad) — the Sangam. Its right-bank tributaries (Chambal, Sind, Betwa, Ken) all rise in the Peninsular Plateau, making the Yamuna unusual: a Himalayan river fed largely by Peninsular tributaries.
- The Brahmaputra is known as the Tsangpo in Tibet, the Siang/Dihang where it enters India in Arunachal, and the Brahmaputra in Assam. It takes a sharp U-turn around Namcha Barwa to enter India. Largest tributary: Subansiri. The Brahmaputra causes annual flooding in Assam because its Tibetan catchment receives snowmelt and monsoon rain simultaneously.
- The Barak River drains the Northeast hill states and is the second-largest river system of NE India. It joins the Meghna in Bangladesh, which in turn meets the Brahmaputra-Ganga delta. Almost all of Mizoram’s north-flowing rivers (Tlawng, Tuirial, Tuivawl) eventually reach the Brahmaputra system via the Barak.
- Mizoram’s longest river is the Tlawng (Dhaleshwari) — ~185 km, flows northward, joins the Barak in Assam. It was historically the main transport route used by the British when they arrived in 1890. The Tuirial is harnessed for hydropower.
- Mizoram’s biggest river is the Chhimtuipui (also Kolodyne or Kaladan). It originates in Chin state, Myanmar, enters Mizoram’s southern districts (Saiha, Lawngtlai), and returns to Myanmar where it reaches the Bay of Bengal at Sittwe. India’s Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project uses this river to connect Mizoram to a deep-sea port in Myanmar.
- The Peninsular rivers are older than the Himalayan rivers and have reached "mature" stage — broad valleys, low gradients, stable courses. They mostly flow east into the Bay of Bengal, where they form large deltas: Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, and Kaveri.
- The Godavari is the longest river in Peninsular India (~1,465 km) — called "Dakshin Ganga" (Ganga of the South). It rises at Trimbakeshwar near Nashik and drains parts of Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh. Major tributaries: Pravara, Manjira, Indravati, Pranhita.
- The Krishna rises at Mahabaleshwar in the Western Ghats and flows ~1,400 km through Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, and Andhra Pradesh. Largest tributary: the Tungabhadra (which itself was the river around which Vijayanagara empire grew).
- The Kaveri / Cauvery rises at Talakaveri in Kodagu (Karnataka), flows through Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, and forms a delta near Thanjavur. Inter-state water sharing between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu has been one of India’s longest-running river disputes.
- Only two major Peninsular rivers flow WEST: the Narmada and the Tapi. Both flow through rift valleys (grabens) between Vindhya-Satpura ranges and drain into the Arabian Sea via estuaries, not deltas. The Narmada rises at Amarkantak (MP); the Tapi at Multai (MP).
- The Narmada traditionally divides North India from South India and runs through a rift valley between the Vindhya range (north) and the Satpura range (south). At ~1,312 km it is the largest west-flowing Peninsular river. Tapi flows almost parallel, just south of Satpura.
- Why no west-flowing river deltas? The west-flowing Peninsular rivers fall into rift valleys with hard-rock margins and short distance to the sea — they don’t spread sediment laterally. The Narmada and Tapi form estuaries instead of deltas.
- Inland drainage: a few rivers don’t reach the sea at all. The Luni in Rajasthan flows into the Rann of Kachchh. Streams from the Aravallis and the Sambhar Salt Lake area drain into inland basins. This is characteristic of the arid west.

chapters.heading: 4. Climate & Monsoon
chapters.body_markdown:
**Overview:** India’s climate zones, the southwest and northeast monsoons, and the key cities shaped by them.

**Core Mental Model:** India’s climate is the monsoon. Two seasonal winds reverse over the Indian Ocean, and that reversal shapes agriculture, settlement, and history.

### India’s Three Cropping Seasons

| Season | Sown → Harvested | High-Yield Crop Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Kharif** (Monsoon) | Jun–Jul → Sep–Oct | Rice (Paddy), Maize, Cotton, Jute, Groundnut, Soyabean |
| **Rabi** (Winter) | Oct–Dec → Mar–Apr | Wheat, Barley, Mustard, Gram, Peas |
| **Zaid** (Summer) | Mar → Jun | Watermelon, Cucumber, Muskmelon, Fodder crops |

**Exam Trap:** Tamil Nadu (Coromandel Coast) receives its **bulk rainfall in Oct–Dec** from the **Retreating (NE) Monsoon**, not the June SW Monsoon!

### High-Yield Exam Facts

- India experiences a tropical monsoon climate, dominated by the seasonal reversal of winds over the Indian Ocean.
- The southwest monsoon (June–September) accounts for about 75% of India’s annual rainfall.
- The Arabian Sea branch strikes the Western Ghats first, producing heavy rain on the windward side and a rain-shadow on the leeward side (the Deccan Plateau).
- The Bay of Bengal branch advances along the Ganga plain and is deflected by the Himalayas, watering northern and eastern India.
- The northeast monsoon (October–December) brings most of Tamil Nadu’s rainfall, since the state lies in the rain-shadow of the Western Ghats during the southwest monsoon.
- Mawsynram and Cherrapunji in Meghalaya are among the wettest places on Earth, due to orographic lift from the Bay of Bengal branch hitting the Khasi Hills.
- Jaisalmer in the Thar Desert receives less than 200 mm of rainfall annually — a tropical dry climate.

chapters.heading: 5. Soils of India
chapters.body_markdown:
**Overview:** The eight major soil types of India and the geology, climate, and crops they dictate.

**Core Mental Model:** Soil is parent rock plus climate plus time. India’s 8 ICAR soil types match almost perfectly onto geology and rainfall — and they decide what grows where.

### Major Indian Soils Quick Match

| Soil Type | Region | Best Known For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Alluvial | Northern Plains & deltas (~40% of India) | Most fertile; Khadar (new) > Bhangar (old) |
| Black (Regur) | Deccan Trap (Maharashtra, MP, Gujarat) | **Cotton**; self-ploughing, high moisture retention |
| Red & Yellow | Eastern & Southern Peninsula | Iron oxide gives red colour; millets & pulses |
| Laterite | Heavy rain Ghats, NE Hills, Kerala | Leached; brick-making, **tea, coffee, cashew** |

### High-Yield Exam Facts

- The Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) classifies Indian soils into 8 major groups: Alluvial, Black, Red & Yellow, Laterite, Arid/Desert, Mountain/Forest, Peaty/Marshy, and Saline/Alkaline. Soil formation depends on CLORPT — Climate, Living organisms, Original parent material, Relief, and Time.
- Alluvial soil is India’s largest soil group, covering about 43% of the country. Found in the Indo-Gangetic-Brahmaputra Plains and along the eastern coastal deltas. Rich in potash (K) and lime, deficient in nitrogen (N) and humus.
- Alluvial soils have two sub-types matching the Northern Plains belts: Khadar (newer alluvium, in flood plains, very fertile, replenished yearly) and Bhangar (older alluvium, terrace tops, contains "kankar" calcareous nodules, less fertile).
- Black soil (locally Regur) formed from weathering of Deccan basalt lava flows. It contains montmorillonite clay, which makes it "self-ploughing" — it shrinks and cracks deeply when dry, then swells when wet, mixing itself. Highly water-retentive. Ideal for cotton.
- Black soil distribution: Maharashtra (the largest spread), Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, northern Karnataka, parts of Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. Crops: cotton (its main association), soybean, jowar, oilseeds, pulses. Rich in lime, iron, magnesia; poor in nitrogen and phosphorus.
- Red & Yellow soils form from weathering of crystalline igneous rocks in low-rainfall regions. The colour comes from iron oxide (red when dehydrated, yellow when hydrated). Found in the eastern and southern Peninsular Plateau: Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, parts of AP, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu. Generally low fertility — needs fertiliser to be productive. Crops: millets, groundnut, potato, pulses.
- Laterite soil forms in regions with high temperature AND heavy seasonal rainfall — the alternation between wet and dry causes severe leaching of silica, leaving behind iron and aluminium oxides (gives the brick-red colour). Found on: Western Ghats summit, parts of Eastern Ghats and Odisha, Northeast hills (including Mizoram and Meghalaya).
- Laterite soils are typically acidic and low in nutrients but are valuable for plantation crops that don’t need fertile soil: tea, coffee, cashew, rubber. Karnataka and Kerala laterite zones are famous for coffee, cashew, and spice plantations.
- Arid (Desert) soils cover western Rajasthan and adjoining Gujarat. Sandy, low in organic matter, often saline. High phosphate content but very low nitrogen. With irrigation (Indira Gandhi Canal) parts have become productive for wheat, barley, and cotton.
- Mountain (Forest) soils occupy the Himalayan slopes and the NE hills. They are shallow, immature, and stony — humus-rich on forest floors, less developed on bare slopes. Mizoram’s steep terrain bears mostly thin mountain/forest soils overlying laterite, supporting bamboo and evergreen forests but limiting settled agriculture.
- Peaty/Marshy soils form in waterlogged areas with high organic accumulation. India’s classic example is Kuttanad in Kerala — a region farmed mostly *below* sea level, where rice is grown on reclaimed wetland. The Sundarbans delta also has peaty soils mixed with saline mud.
- Saline/Alkaline soils (locally Reh, Kallar, or Usar) develop where salts accumulate at the surface — typically in arid regions with poor drainage, or in over-irrigated areas where rising groundwater brings salts up by capillary action. Found in the Rann of Kachchh and patches of western UP, Punjab, and Haryana.
- Reclamation of saline soils: gypsum application (replaces Na⁺ with Ca²⁺), improved drainage, and leaching with fresh water. The Central Soil Salinity Research Institute at Karnal leads this work.
- Mizoram-specific: the state’s steep terrain and heavy rainfall produce extensive lateritic and mountain/forest soils. Combined with jhum (shifting cultivation), erosion is a major concern. Terrace farming on contour lines is increasingly used to retain soil and water on the slopes.

chapters.heading: 6. Forests & Protected Areas
chapters.body_markdown:
**Overview:** India’s forest cover, biodiversity hotspots, national parks, tiger reserves, and biosphere reserves.

**Core Mental Model:** India protects nature in concentric layers — sanctuaries for species, parks for landscapes, tiger reserves for whole food chains, biosphere reserves for ecosystems including humans. The northeast (especially Mizoram) carries the highest forest cover by percentage.

### High-Frequency Biosphere Reserves (Match the Following)

| Biosphere Reserve | State / Region | Exam Highlight |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nilgiri (1986) | TN / Kerala / Karnataka | India’s **first** Biosphere Reserve; Western Ghats hotspot |
| Nanda Devi | Uttarakhand | Himalayan alpine flora |
| Manas | Assam | UNESCO World Heritage; Golden Langur & Pygmy Hog |
| Nokrek | Meghalaya | Garo Hills; Red Panda & citrus gene pool |
| Simlipal | Odisha | Tiger reserve & elephants |
| Sundarbans | West Bengal | World’s largest mangrove forest; Royal Bengal Tiger |

### High-Yield Exam Facts

- India’s total forest and tree cover is 25.17% of the geographical area (ISFR 2023). Forest cover alone is 21.76%; tree cover (small patches, agroforestry) is 3.41%. The National Forest Policy 1988 targets 33% — the country is still well below that.
- States with the highest forest cover by AREA: Madhya Pradesh (77,073 km²) leads, then Arunachal Pradesh (65,882 km²) and Chhattisgarh (55,812 km²). States with the highest forest cover by PERCENTAGE: Lakshadweep (91.33%), Mizoram (85.34%), Andaman & Nicobar (81.62%).
- Eight states/UTs have over 75% forest cover: Lakshadweep, Mizoram, A&N Islands, Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Meghalaya, Tripura, Manipur — mostly the northeast. The NE region as a whole has 67% forest cover, far above the national average.
- Mizoram is in a special position. It has the maximum INCREASE in forest cover in ISFR 2023 (+242 km²) AND the 2nd highest cover by percentage. Combined with declining cover in neighbouring NE states, Mizoram is becoming the green anchor of the region.
- Protected Areas in India come in four legal categories under the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972: National Parks (IUCN Cat II), Wildlife Sanctuaries (IUCN Cat IV), Conservation Reserves, and Community Reserves. Together they cover ~5.28% of India.
- India has approximately 106 National Parks (number varies slightly across sources and updates). Jim Corbett (Uttarakhand, established 1936) is the oldest. Madhya Pradesh has the most national parks. Hemis NP in Ladakh is the largest by area.
- Project Tiger was launched on 1 April 1973 by PM Indira Gandhi after a 1972 census revealed only 1,800 tigers remained (from ~40,000 a century earlier). It started with 9 reserves; today there are 58 tiger reserves covering ~84,500 km².
- India’s 2022 tiger census counted 3,682 wild tigers — about 70-75% of the world’s wild tiger population. Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra have 6 tiger reserves each (the most). Corbett Tiger Reserve has the highest tiger population and density.
- Mizoram’s Dampa Tiger Reserve (declared 1994) is in western Mizoram, bordering Bangladesh. Core area ~500 km². It is the largest wildlife sanctuary in Mizoram. Tiger numbers here are low — the reserve has struggled with shifting cultivation and a border fence that blocks tiger movement.
- India has 18 Biosphere Reserves; 12 of them are part of UNESCO’s Man and Biosphere (MAB) network. Each has three concentric zones: Core (strictly protected), Buffer (research and tourism), and Transition (sustainable human use).
- Nilgiri (Tamil Nadu – Karnataka – Kerala) was India’s FIRST biosphere reserve (1986). It hosts the largest tiger population in South Asia across Bandipur, Nagarhole, Mudumalai, and Wayanad.
- India has FOUR of the world’s 36 biodiversity hotspots: (1) Western Ghats & Sri Lanka, (2) Eastern Himalayas, (3) Indo-Burma (which includes Mizoram and most of NE India), (4) Sundaland (the Nicobar Islands). Mizoram falls squarely in the Indo-Burma hotspot.
- Famous one-off conservation facts often asked: Kaziranga (Assam, UNESCO WHS) hosts ~70% of the world’s one-horned rhinos. Gir (Gujarat) is the only remaining home of the Asiatic lion. Sundarbans has the only swimming tigers (salt-adapted). Kanha (MP) inspired Kipling’s Jungle Book. Silent Valley (Kerala) was saved from a dam in the 1980s.
- Mizoram has 2 National Parks: Phawngpui (Blue Mountain) NP and Murlen NP. Phawngpui surrounds the highest peak in Mizoram. Murlen lies near Champhai in eastern Mizoram, with evergreen sub-tropical forest.
- India’s mangrove cover is ~4,992 km² (0.15% of geographical area). The Sundarbans (West Bengal) is the world’s largest mangrove forest. Mangroves are critical against cyclones, coastal erosion, and carbon storage.

chapters.heading: 7. Geography of Mizoram
chapters.body_markdown:
**Overview:** Ridges, three river families, lakes, geology & climate — GS-V Unit II.

**Core Mental Model:** Mizoram is 90%+ structural hills aligned north–south. That grain sorts every river into three families — north to the Barak (Tlawng), south to the Kaladan (Chhimtuipui), west to the Karnaphuli (Khawthlangtuipui).

### Mizoram’s Three River Families & Key Landmarks

| Family / Feature | Direction & Basin | Key Rivers / Details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| North-flowing | → Barak (Assam) | **Tlawng** (longest in Mizoram, ~185 km), Tuirial, Tuivawl, Teirei |
| South-flowing | → Kaladan (Myanmar) | **Chhimtuipui** (Kaladan), Mat, Tuichang, Tiau (India–Myanmar border) |
| West-flowing | → Karnaphuli (Bangladesh) | **Khawthlangtuipui**, Tuichawng, Kau |
| Peaks & Lakes | Highest / Largest | **Phawngpui** (Blue Mountain, 2,157 m, Lawngtlai) · **Palak Dil** (largest natural lake, Siaha) · **Tam Dil** (Saitual) |

**Memory Hook:** Remember Mizoram’s borders: **3 Indian states** (Assam, Manipur, Tripura) and **2 countries** (Myanmar to east/south, Bangladesh to west). The **Tropic of Cancer (23.5°N)** passes right through Mizoram near Thenzawl!

### High-Yield Exam Facts

- Vitals: 21°56′–24°31′ N, 92°16′–93°26′ E; area 21,081 sq km (0.64% of India); the Tropic of Cancer crosses the state. Stretch: 277 km N–S, 121 km E–W. International borders: Myanmar 404 km, Bangladesh 318 km; national borders with Manipur, Assam, Tripura total 146.6 km.
- Terrain: 90.5% structural hills, 6.4% linear ridges, only 3.1% floodplains and valley fills. Altitude runs 400–2,157 m (average ~1,000 m); ridges are N–S aligned and WESTERN slopes are steeper than eastern. Forest cover: 85.34% (ISFR 2023) — among India’s highest.
- Ranges to name: Sialkal (NE, on the Manipur–Myanmar border), Chalfilh and Hmuifang (Aizawl district), Reiek (Mamit), and Phawngpui (Lawngtlai) — the Blue Mountain, 2,157 m, the state’s highest point.
- North-flowing family (→ Barak system): TLAWNG is the longest at 185.5 km — rises at Zopui Hill (Lunglei), splits the state into two nearly equal halves, and is called the Dhaleswari in Cachar (Assam). Tributaries include Tut and Teirei. Tuirial (~117 km, partially navigable) and Tuivawl (~72 km) also flow north.
- South-flowing family: CHHIMTUIPUI (Kaladan) is the largest river by water volume — it rises in western Myanmar near Sabawngte, flows ~138 km, and forms the international boundary with Myanmar. Dendritic pattern; tributaries Tuichang, Tuichawng, Mat, Mengpui. TIAU (~159 km) is the natural boundary with Myanmar in the east.
- West-flowing family: KHAWTHLANGTUIPUI (Karnaphuli) drains the southwest — rises at Saithah (Mamit), runs ~128 km, enters Bangladesh near Tlabung, and forms the natural boundary with Bangladesh. Tributaries: Kawrpui, Tuichawng, Phairuang, Kau, De. Strategic trade route to Chittagong.
- Lakes formed where hills and ridges act as embankments — large: Palak, Tamdil, Rengdil; smaller: Rungdil, Vachadil. Plains are only ~3% and inter-montane: Champhai (largest — wet rice), Serchhip plains, the Northern plains, and Chamdur (western Siaha).
- Geology: longitudinal anticlines and synclines control drainage and slopes; BIS (2016) puts Mizoram in SEISMIC ZONE V; the Indo-Myanmar tectonic arc passes through Siaha district. Tertiary sandstones and shales; marine fossils near Lunglei. Stratigraphy (ascending): Barail → Surma (Bhuban + Bokabil — Bokabil holds petroleum) → Tipam (youngest, coarse sandstone).
- Climate & vegetation: tropical to temperate-montane; 10–30 °C (avg 22 °C); ~2,394 mm rain a year, ~40% of it in July–August; three seasons, the rainy one running nearly six months (mid-May to late Oct). Forests: Tropical Wet-Evergreen (west), Tropical Semi-Evergreen (~50% of area, central belt), Mountain Sub-Tropical on the high eastern fringe. Minerals: sandstone widespread, limestone in patches, coal at Kolasib/Thinglian, petroleum confirmed at Bilkhawthlir, uranium potential in Middle Bhuban sandstones (~4 ppm).
