chapters.heading: 8. World: The Restless Earth
chapters.body_markdown:
**Overview:** Ring of Fire, quake belts, fold vs block mountains, volcanism.

**Core Mental Model:** The Circum-Pacific “Ring of Fire” alone accounts for ~68% of all earthquakes — quakes, volcanoes and young fold mountains all cluster on the same convergent plate boundaries.

**Exam Trap:** **Tsunamis** are triggered primarily by **undersea earthquakes** (vertical seafloor displacement at subduction zones) or submarine volcanic eruptions — NOT by surface winds or tides.

### High-Yield Exam Facts

- Mountains cover ~27% of the world’s land surface, supply up to 80% of the planet’s fresh surface water, house ~12% of humanity (FAO) — and over 50% of people depend directly or indirectly on mountain resources.
- Three-way classification: FOLD mountains form at convergent plate boundaries (Himalayas, Alps, Rockies, Andes); BLOCK mountains form by tension and faulting — the uplifted block is a HORST, the dropped valley a GRABEN (Sierra Nevada, Black Forest); VOLCANIC mountains are “mountains of accumulation” built from erupted material.
- Earthquake anatomy: energy releases at the FOCUS (hypocentre) inside the earth; the point on the surface directly above is the EPICENTRE. Most shallow quakes are sudden stress release along a fault rupture.
- Shadow zones — how we know the core: P-waves go missing between 103° and 142° from the epicentre; S-waves vanish beyond 103° entirely (they cannot cross the liquid outer core). Beyond 142° only P-waves reappear. The 103°–142° band is the shadow zone for BOTH wave types.
- The Circum-Pacific Belt — the “Pacific Ring of Fire” — accounts for about 68% of all earthquakes and hugs heavily populated coasts. It is a chain of subduction zones: converging plates dive, melt, and feed explosive volcanoes.
- Volcanism 101: magma from the upper mantle reaches the surface as LAVA plus ash, gases and rock fragments. Eruption style (explosive vs effusive) depends on magma composition, gas content and volcano structure. Divergent boundaries produce fissure-type volcanoes and mid-ocean ridges; convergent boundaries produce subduction-zone volcanoes.
- Tsunami logic: an undersea quake suddenly displaces the water column; waves race across open ocean and rear up in shallow coastal water. Depth of focus sets the warning delay — roughly 60–90 seconds between P-wave arrival and the destructive shaking.

chapters.heading: 9. World: Atmosphere & Heat Zones
chapters.body_markdown:
**Overview:** Five layers overhead, three heat zones on the map, one heat budget.

**Core Mental Model:** Sunlight arrives at an angle — latitude decides everything. The torrid, temperate and frigid zones are just the geometry of the overhead sun; the atmosphere’s five layers and the heat budget do the rest.

### High-Yield Exam Facts

- Atmosphere composition: nitrogen ~78%, oxygen ~21%, argon ~0.93%, CO₂ ~0.04% — but the climatic action lives in the minor players: WATER VAPOUR, particulate matter (dust as condensation nuclei), CO₂ and OZONE, which absorb and re-radiate heat.
- Five layers, ascending: TROPOSPHERE (up to ~18 km over the equator, ~8 km at poles — thickest where heating is greatest) — ALL weather (cyclones, clouds, rain) happens here; the TROPOPAUSE caps it. STRATOSPHERE (to 50 km): temperature RISES with height because ozone absorbs UV — jets fly in its calm lower reaches; the OZONOSPHERE spans the stratosphere and lower mesosphere. MESOSPHERE: coldest layer — meteors burn here. THERMOSPHERE/IONOSPHERE: radio waves reflect. EXOSPHERE: fades to space.
- INSOLATION = incoming solar radiation. Factors: (1) solar output — the ~11-year sunspot cycle swings it between ~1340 and 1380 W/m²; (2) ANGLE OF INCIDENCE — insolation falls as latitude rises (slanting rays spread over more area and cross more atmosphere); (3) duration of day; (4) distance from the sun — perihelion (Jan, nearest) vs aphelion (July, farthest); (5) transparency of the atmosphere.
- HEAT BUDGET: the earth keeps a constant temperature because heat received (insolation) exactly equals heat lost (terrestrial radiation). Of 100 units arriving: roughly a third is reflected straight back (ALBEDO — clouds, ice, dust); the rest is absorbed by atmosphere and surface, then returned as long-wave terrestrial radiation. The atmosphere is heated mainly FROM BELOW — by terrestrial radiation, conduction and convection — not directly by sunlight.
- The three heat zones are pure geometry: TORRID zone (23½°N–23½°S) — the overhead sun visits at least once a year; TEMPERATE zones (23½°–66½°) — never overhead, always slanting; FRIGID zones (66½°–poles) — the sun barely climbs, and inside the polar circles you get midnight sun and polar night.
- The TROPIC OF CANCER threads India through eight states — Gujarat, Rajasthan, MP, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and MIZORAM — the same line you saw in the Mizoram chapter. Latitude connects the world map to the home map.

chapters.heading: 10. World: Winds, Belts & Currents
chapters.body_markdown:
**Overview:** Seven pressure belts → planetary winds → ocean gyres → El Niño.

**Core Mental Model:** One engine, three layers: pressure belts make the planetary winds, the winds drag the oceans into gyres (warm poleward, cold equatorward), and a hiccup in the Pacific limb of this engine is El Niño.

### High-Yield Exam Facts

- Air has weight — that weight is atmospheric pressure; isobars join points of equal pressure. Warm air expands, gets lighter and rises (low pressure); cold air compresses, densifies and sinks (high pressure). Wind is simply air moving from high to low.
- Seven belts, alternating: Equatorial Low (intense heating, rising air, daily thunderstorms — the calm “doldrums”); Sub-tropical Highs to ~35° (air sinking after the Hadley circuit — hot deserts and the “horse latitudes”); Sub-polar Lows (45°–polar circles, where sub-tropical and polar winds converge and rise); Polar Highs (cold dense sinking air).
- Tri-cellular model: the HADLEY cell (largest, equator to ~30–40°) drives the trade winds; the FERREL cell (middle, moves opposite — “like a cog in a machine” between the other two) gives the westerlies; the POLAR cell (smallest, weakest) gives the polar easterlies.
- Coriolis: because Earth’s surface spins fastest at the equator, moving air and water deflect RIGHT in the northern hemisphere and LEFT in the southern. That is why the trades arrive as NE trades (north) and SE trades (south), and why ocean gyres spin clockwise in the north and anticlockwise in the south.
- Trade winds are descending and stable at their origin (sub-tropical highs); where the two hemispheres’ trades meet at the equator, the air rises into storms. Their eastern flanks ride over cool ocean and stay dry — which is why deserts hug the western coasts of continents in the trade-wind belt.
- Currents come in two families: WARM (originate near the equator, flow poleward, high surface temperature) and COLD (originate polewards, flow toward the equator). Drivers: planetary winds (the biggest), Coriolis, temperature (an ~8 cm sea-surface gradient from equator to mid-latitudes!), salinity (denser saline water sinks), and coastline shape.
- Name-drop set for prelims — warm: Gulf Stream→North Atlantic Drift, Kuroshio, Brazil (the South Equatorial current splits in two on Brazil’s shoulder), Agulhas, East Australian. Cold: Labrador, Canary, Benguela, Peru/Humboldt, Oyashio, California. Where Labrador meets the Gulf Stream: fog + the great Newfoundland fishing grounds.
- Normal Pacific year: high pressure sits off Peru, low over Indonesia/N. Australia — strong easterly trades push warm water west (rain in Indonesia), while cold nutrient-rich water UPWELLS off Peru (rich fisheries).
- EL NIÑO year (irregular, every 2–7 years, avg ~3–4): pressure drops over the central Pacific and South America’s coast, trades weaken, the Peru current runs warm, upwelling collapses — rain shifts to the Peruvian coast while Indonesia/Australia (and often the Indian monsoon) dry out. LA NIÑA is the cold overcorrection of the same see-saw.

chapters.heading: 11. World: Resources & Industry
chapters.body_markdown:
**Overview:** Why industry sits where it does — iron, coal, copper, oil belts mapped.

**Core Mental Model:** Industry sits where its inputs are cheapest to assemble — so every great industrial region is parked on a coalfield, an ore belt, or a port. Map the minerals first and the factory regions locate themselves.

### High-Yield Exam Facts

- Location factors, geographical: raw materials (steel near ore), power (coal/hydro/oil), transport (roads, rail, PORTS), labour (skilled or cheap — textiles chase workforces), water (iron & steel, textiles, chemicals are thirsty), flat land and moderate climate, market proximity (consumer goods).
- Non-geographical factors: capital and loans, investment climate, government policy (subsidised power, tax breaks, siting rules against pollution and over-clustering), pressure groups — and INDUSTRIAL INERTIA: the tendency of industry to stay put even after its original locational advantage is gone.
- Sector logic: PRIMARY industries (mining, forestry, agriculture) sit on the resource itself; SECONDARY (manufacturing) minimises assembly cost of materials + energy + labour; TERTIARY (services) follows market demand and population density. Industrialisation then grows the towns around it.
- Classic industrial regions: RUHR (Germany) — the coal–steel template; GREAT LAKES (N. America) — Mesabi iron meets Appalachian coal on cheap lake transport; MANCHURIA — China’s biggest coal industry, Anshan steel; NORTHERN KYUSHU — Japan’s coal–steel cradle; in India, the CHOTANAGPUR plateau (steel–cement–paper: Jamshedpur, Hazaribagh) and the market-driven DELHI NCR belt (textiles, leather, pharma, consumer goods).
- IRON ORE (world reserves ~3,20,000 million tonnes): N. America (Great Lakes, Labrador), Russia–Kazakhstan (Urals, Magnitogorsk), Brazil (Carajas, Itabira, Minas Gerais), Australia (Koolyanobbing, Iron Knob/Iron Duke), Europe (Lorraine, S. Wales), Africa (Transvaal, Liberia), China (Manchuria, Anshan).
- IRON ORE, India — ~95% of reserves in Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Goa, TN, AP, Telangana. Belts: Odisha (Sundergarh, Mayurbhanj); Jharkhand (oldest mines — Noamundi & Gua in Singhbhum); Chhattisgarh (Durg, Dantewada, BAILADILA); Karnataka (Sandur–Hospet in Ballari, Baba Budan hills, Kudremukh); plus Goa, Maharashtra (Chandrapur, Ratnagiri) and Tamil Nadu (Salem, Nilgiris).
- COAL — the most UNEVENLY distributed mineral; used for thermal power and smelting. China (Shansi, Fushun, Shenyang), USA (Appalachia: Kentucky, Illinois…), Europe (Ruhr, Upper Silesia, Durham), Russia (Moscow, Ob & Lena basins), Australia (Newcastle), Africa (Transvaal, Natal). India: JHARIA, BOKARO, RANIGANJ on the Damodar; Korba, Singrauli, Talcher, Singareni; NEYVELI = lignite.
- COPPER — CHILE leads with ~27% of world output (Escondida and Collahuasi are among the biggest mines on earth); PERU next (~10%). India: Singhbhum (Jharkhand), Balaghat (MP), Jhunjhunu & Alwar (Rajasthan). Resources split: RENEWABLE (solar, wind — replenish fast) vs NON-RENEWABLE (coal, petroleum, gas — fixed stock, millennia to renew).

title: Indian, World & Mizoram History
summary: 11 chronological History chapters with site/dynasty/revolt tables, Mizoram’s statehood timeline (1871–1987), and exam traps — linked directly to Atlas maps, Chronicle, and 962+ History PYQs.

chapters.heading: 1. Indus Valley Civilization
chapters.body_markdown:
**Overview:** Bronze Age cities on the Indus — sites, rivers, excavators, extremes.

**Core Mental Model:** Every IVC exam question is secretly a map question: pin each site to its river, its excavator, and its direction on the map — Manda north, Daimabad south, Sutkagendor west, Alamgirpur east.

### IVC Major Sites · River · Excavator

| Site | River | Excavator & Year | Signature Find |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Harappa | Ravi | Dayaram Sahni (1921) | Granaries, first site excavated |
| Mohenjodaro | Indus | R.D. Banerji (1922) | Great Bath, Bronze Dancing Girl, Pashupati seal |
| Lothal (Gujarat) | Bhogava | S.R. Rao (1954) | World’s earliest tidal **dockyard**, rice husks |
| Kalibangan (Rajasthan) | Ghaggar | A. Ghosh / B.B. Lal | Ploughed field, fire altars |
| Dholavira (Gujarat) | Luni basin | R.S. Bisht | UNESCO site; 3-part town & water reservoirs |

**Memory Hook:** IVC 4 geographical extremes: **North** Manda (J&K) · **South** Daimabad (Maharashtra) · **West** Sutkagendor (Balochistan) · **East** Alamgirpur (UP).

### High-Yield Exam Facts

- The IVC belongs to the Bronze Age and to the Proto-history of India. Its contemporaries were Mesopotamia (Tigris–Euphrates), Egypt (Nile), and China (Hwang Ho). Phases: Early 3500–2600 BC, Mature 2600–1900 BC, Late 1900–1500 BC.
- Discovery chain: Charles Masson noticed the ruins in 1826; Alexander Cunningham collected seals five decades later; Dayaram Sahni excavated Harappa in 1921 (banks of the Ravi); R.D. Banerji excavated Mohenjodaro (“mound of the dead”) in 1922 on the Indus; in 1924 John Marshall named it the Indus Valley Civilization.
- Extremes — memorize as a compass: Manda in Jammu (river Chenab) is the northernmost site, Daimabad in Maharashtra (river Pravara) the southernmost, Sutkagendor on the Makran coast the westernmost, Alamgirpur in western U.P. the easternmost. Shortugai in Afghanistan was a distant trade outpost.
- Superlatives: Mohenjodaro is the largest site overall; Rakhigarhi (Haryana) is the largest site in India; Harappa and Mohenjodaro were the “capital cities”; Lothal and Sutkagendor were port cities.
- Town planning: grid system with streets at right angles; the raised Citadel on the western mound housed public buildings and the ruling class, the lower eastern town housed common people; brilliant covered drains of mortar, lime and gypsum. The Great Bath (with bitumen-lined bed) and a granary stand at Mohenjodaro; Harappa also had granaries.
- Economy: main crops wheat and barley; rice evidence at Lothal and Rangpur; world’s first ploughed field found at Kalibangan; the Indus people were the first in the world to produce cotton (Greeks called it Sindon). Trade with Mesopotamia was by barter — no coins; Sumerian texts call the Indus region “Meluha”.
- Things the Harappans did NOT know — a favourite trick question: iron, the horse (debated), the lion, and sugarcane. Weights were made of limestone and steatite, usually cubical.

chapters.heading: 2. The Vedic Age
chapters.body_markdown:
**Overview:** Sapta Sindhu river names, Rig Vedic society, and the eastward shift.

**Core Mental Model:** The Rig Veda is a map: Sapta Sindhu is the Punjab river system under older names (Vitasta=Jhelum, Asikni=Chenab, Parushni=Ravi, Vipasha=Beas, Shutudri=Sutlej). Then, 1000–500 BC, the whole civilization slides east down the Ganga.

### The Four Vedas & Six Vedangas

| Veda | Focus | Key Fact |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rigveda | Hymns (1,028 suktas) | Oldest; contains **Gayatri Mantra** (3rd Mandala) |
| Samaveda | Chants & melodies | Origin of Indian classical music |
| Yajurveda | Sacrificial rituals | Prose + verse (Shukla & Krishna) |
| Atharvaveda | Charms, medicine, daily life | Added last |
| **Six Vedangas** | Auxiliary limbs | *Shiksha, Kalpa, Vyakarana, Nirukta, Chhanda, Jyotisha* |

### High-Yield Exam Facts

- The Vedic people — Indo-European speakers believed to originate in the Steppes of southern Russia and Central Asia — appeared in India a little before 1500 BC, migrating in waves. Periods: Early/Rig Vedic 1500–1000 BC (Sapta Sindhu, late Bronze–early Iron), Later Vedic 1000–500 BC (Ganga–Yamuna valleys).
- The Rig Veda — the earliest Indo-European text — mentions about 40 rivers. The exam pairs: Vitasta=Jhelum, Asikni=Chenab, Parushni=Ravi, Vipasha=Beas, Shutudri=Sutlej, plus the Sindhu (Indus) and the Saraswati (the “lost” Ghaggar). The Battle of Ten Kings (Dasarajna) was fought on the Parushni — the Ravi.
- Rig Vedic economy: primarily PASTORAL — the cow was the chief wealth and unit of exchange, most wars were fought over cattle; agriculture was secondary. Horses and spoke-wheeled chariots were their signature technology (both unknown to the Harappans — a favourite contrast question). No clear evidence of trade or coins.
- Polity: the tribe (Jana/Vis) under a hereditary chief, the RAJAN, checked by assemblies — SABHA (council of elders), SAMITI (national assembly; even elected the Rajan in traces), VIDATHA and GANA. Women attended Sabha and Vidatha in the early period. Bali = voluntary offering, not tax; no standing army. Purohita (Vasishtha the conservative, Vishvamitra the liberal) was the key functionary; Senani led the army; Gramani headed the village.
- Society: patriarchal, kinship-based; Kula/Griha = family; Vis divided into gramas — when gramas clashed it was SAMGRAMA (the literal origin of the word for war). Monogamy prevailed, widow remarriage existed, and there is no evidence of child marriage in the Rig Vedic period.
- Later Vedic changes (1000–500 BC): iron (shyama ayas) clears the Ganga forests; agriculture overtakes cattle; territory replaces tribe (Rashtra appears); the varna order hardens; Sabha and Samiti fade before rising kingship. Painted Grey Ware pottery marks the doab settlements like Hastinapura. This eastward world is the stage on which the Mahajanapadas rise.
- Vedic literature ladder: 4 Vedas (Rig — hymns; Sama — melodies; Yajur — rituals; Atharva — charms) → Brahmanas (ritual explanation) → Aranyakas (forest books) → Upanishads (philosophy; “Satyameva Jayate” comes from the Mundaka Upanishad). The Gayatri mantra is addressed to the solar deity Savitri.

chapters.heading: 3. Buddhism & Jainism
chapters.body_markdown:
**Overview:** Buddha’s life-map, the four councils, Mahavira and the Jain sites.

**Core Mental Model:** Buddha’s biography is eight pins on one small map — and every Buddhist council sits on the Magadha–Vaishali circuit you already know from the Mahajanapadas chapter. Same geography, new religion.

### The Four Buddhist Councils

| Council | Place | Patron King | President / Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1st (483 BC) | Rajagriha | Ajatashatru | Mahakassapa; Vinaya & Sutta Pitaka compiled |
| 2nd (383 BC) | Vaishali | Kalasoka | Sabakami; split into Sthaviravadins & Mahasanghikas |
| 3rd (250 BC) | Pataliputra | **Ashoka** | Moggaliputta Tissa; Abhidhamma Pitaka |
| 4th (72 AD) | Kashmir (Kundalvana) | **Kanishka** | Vasumitra; **Hinayana & Mahayana** split |

### High-Yield Exam Facts

- Gautama Buddha — also Siddhartha, Shakyamuni, Tathagata — born 563 BC at LUMBINI (Nepal) in the Shakya Kshatriya clan of Kapilavastu. Father Suddhodhana, mother Mahamaya (a Koshalan princess); raised by his aunt Mahaprajapati Gautami; wife Yashodhara, son Rahul; teachers Alara Kalama and Udraka Ramaputra; horse Kanthaka.
- The four sights (old man, sick man, corpse, ascetic) drove him out at 29. Enlightenment at 35 at BODH GAYA, under a pipal tree on the banks of the Phalgu, on the 49th day of meditation. First sermon at SARNATH near Varanasi to five disciples — the Dharma-chakra-pravartana, “turning the wheel of law”. Died 483 BC at 80 at KUSHINAGAR (UP) under a sal tree.
- Core doctrine: Buddhism recognizes neither God nor soul (atma). FOUR NOBLE TRUTHS: the world is full of sorrow; desire causes it; conquering desire removes it (nirvana); the way is the EIGHTFOLD PATH (Ashtangika Marga: right observation, speech, determination, livelihood, memory, action, exercise, meditation). TRIRATNA: Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha.
- Four councils — memorize ruler + dynasty + place: 483 BC Rajgir (Ajatashatru, Haryanka); 383 BC Vaishali (Kalashoka, Shishunaga; president Sabakami); 250 BC Pataliputra (Ashoka, Maurya); AD 72 Kashmir (Kanishka, Kushan) — where the MAHAYANA doctrine was finalized. Literature: the Tripitakas, in PALI.
- Jainism: founded by Rishabhanath (1st tirthankara); 23rd Parshvanath; 24th VARDHAMANA MAHAVIRA — “Jina”, the conqueror — born near Vaishali (Kundagrama), father Siddhartha, mother Trishala; attained Kaivalya (supreme knowledge) at 42; first sermon at PAVA, where he also died (468 BC).
- Jain doctrine: Triratna = right faith, right knowledge, right conduct. FIVE VOWS: ahimsa, satya (non-lying), asteya (non-stealing), aparigraha (non-possession), brahmacharya — the fifth added by Mahavira to Parshvanath’s four. Sects after the Magadha famine: SVETAMBARA (white-clad, Sthulabhadra) and DIGAMBARA (sky-clad, Bhadrabahu — who took Chandragupta Maurya south to Shravanabelagola).
- Why here, why now? Both faiths rose in the 6th-century-BC Mahajanapada world — iron-age surplus, new cities, trade wealth, and Kshatriya resentment of Brahmana ritual cost. Both founders were Kshatriyas from the same Magadha–Vaishali region — the identical geography of the Rise-of-Magadha chapter.

chapters.heading: 4. Mahajanapadas → Mauryas
chapters.body_markdown:
**Overview:** 16 states, the rise of Magadha, and Ashoka’s empire of Dhamma.

**Core Mental Model:** Sixteen Mahajanapadas contested the Gangetic plain; Magadha absorbed them all. The Mauryan climax — and the moral pivot of Indian history — happened on the map at Kalinga, 261 BC.

### High-Yield Exam Facts

- The 16 Mahajanapadas are listed in Buddhist and Jain literature; the period is called the Second Urbanisation, and silver/copper punch-marked coins appear. States were of two kinds: monarchical and republican. Vajji (Vaishali) was the most important republic; the Lichchhavis of Vaishali are called the first republic.
- The real contest was among four: Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa, and Avanti. Magadha (capital Rajgir) won — founded by Brihadratha/Jarasandha, its growth began under the Haryanka dynasty, expanded under the Shishunagas and Nandas, and peaked under the Mauryas.
- Haryanka kings to remember: Bimbisara (matrimonial alliances, annexed Anga), Ajatashatru (war with Vajji, first Buddhist council patronage), Udayin (founded Pataliputra at the Ganga–Son confluence — moving the capital from hill-ringed Rajgir to the river highway).
- The Nandas (344–323 BC) under Dhanananda were fabulously rich and unpopular — the empire Alexander’s soldiers refused to face. Chandragupta Maurya (324/321–297 BC), guided by Kautilya, overthrew them, then defeated Seleucus Nicator, gaining territories up to the Hindu Kush.
- Ashoka (273–232 BC) ruled nearly the whole subcontinent except the extreme south — including Afghanistan, Baluchistan, Kashmir and the Nepal valleys. The Kalinga War (261 BC, 9th regnal year) converted him: from Bherighosha (drum of war) to Dhammaghosha (drum of righteousness). He embraced Buddhism under Upagupta and sent Mahendra and Sanghamitra to Ceylon with a Bodhi sapling.
- Edicts cheat-sheet: Major Rock Edict XIII describes the Kalinga victory and names five Greek kings (Antiochus, Ptolemy, Magas, Antigonus, Alexander of Epirus); Edict IV = Dhammaghosha over Bherighosha; Edict II mentions the Pandyas, Cholas and Keralaputras plus medical care for humans and animals; Pillar Edict VII sums up Ashoka’s Dhamma work.
- Ashoka’s Dhamma was not a sect — it was a civic code: respect elders, mercy to slaves and servants, truth, non-violence, tolerance of all sects. Dhamma Mahamatras were a special cadre appointed to spread it (Rock Edict V).

chapters.heading: 5. Medieval India: Gateway Battles
chapters.body_markdown:
**Overview:** 712–1576: Sindh, Somnath, Tarain, Panipat, Khanwa, Haldighati — one corridor, five centuries.

**Core Mental Model:** The Delhi Sultanate was born on the battlefield of Tarain (1192) and ended a few miles away at Panipat (1526). Learn the corridor once and every medieval battle question becomes a map question.

### High-Yield Exam Facts

- Before the Turks: the Tripartite Struggle. Pratiharas (west), Palas (Bengal) and Rashtrakutas (Deccan) fought a three-way, century-long contest for Kannauj — the symbolic capital of north India. All three exhausted themselves, opening the door to invaders.
- 712 AD: Al-Hajjaj, governor of Iraq, sent Muhammad-bin-Qasim, who defeated Dahir of Sindh at the Battle of Rewar. Qasim called Multan “the City of Gold”. His end was grim — recalled and tortured to death after Hajjaj’s fall.
- Mahmud of Ghazni raided India 17 times (1000–1027) for plunder, not empire — climaxing with the sack of the Somnath temple on the Kathiawar coast in 1025. Contrast with Muhammad of Ghori, who came to STAY.
- Tarain, the double battle: 1191 — Prithviraj Chauhan defeats Ghori. 1192 — Ghori returns and crushes the combined Rajput forces. Turkish rule in India begins with the Second Battle of Tarain; Ghori’s slave Qutb-ud-din Aibak founds the Sultanate in 1206. (Iltutmish later won his own battle of Tarain, c. 1215, against Yaldauz.)
- Sultanate = five dynasties: Slave/Mamluk (1206–90), Khalji (1290–1320), Tughlaq (1320–14), Sayyid (1414–51), Lodi (1451–1526). It ended when Babur defeated and killed Ibrahim Lodi at the FIRST Battle of Panipat, 21 April 1526 — born at Tarain, dead at Panipat, a few miles apart.
- Babur’s follow-up: Khanwa (1527) against Rana Sanga of Mewar — same tactics as Panipat (artillery + tulughma flanking) — secured the Mughal foothold against the Rajput confederacy.
- The Sur interruption: Sher Khan smashed Humayun at Chausa (1539) and again at Bilgram/Kanauj (1540), exiling him 15 years. Sher Shah Suri built the Sur Empire from Sasaram — and the Grand Trunk Road. Humayun returned in 1555, then died in 1556 falling down his library stairs.
- Second Panipat (1556): 13-year-old Akbar’s regent Bairam Khan defeats Hemu Vikramaditya, wazir of Adil Shah, leading the Afghan forces. Akbar had been crowned at Kalanaur the same year. The Mughal restoration is sealed on the SAME battlefield as 1526.
- Akbar in Rajasthan: Chittor — “the key to central Rajasthan” — fell in 1568 after a 6-month siege (Jaimal and Patta commanded; Udai Singh withdrew to the hills). Ranthambhore and Kalinjar followed. At Haldighati (1576), Man Singh’s Mughal army severely defeated Rana Pratap of Mewar — who nonetheless fought on from the hills.

chapters.heading: 6. Delhi Sultanate: Five Dynasties
chapters.body_markdown:
**Overview:** Slave → Khalji → Tughlaq → Sayyid → Lodi — rulers, reforms, experiments.

**Core Mental Model:** One city, five dynasties, 320 years (1206–1526). The Sultanate’s story is a set of experiments radiating from Delhi — Alauddin’s market control, Tughlaq’s capital shift and token currency — and every experiment snaps back to Delhi.

### Five Dynasties of Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526)

| Dynasty | Period | Founder | Key Exam Anchor |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Slave (Mamluk) | 1206–1290 | Qutb-ud-din Aibak | Qutb Minar; Iltutmish (Iqta); Razia Sultan; Balban |
| Khilji | 1290–1320 | Jalal-ud-din Khilji | Alauddin Khilji — market price control & dagh/chehra |
| Tughlaq | 1320–1414 | Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq | Muhammad bin Tughlaq (Daulatabad, token currency) |
| Sayyid | 1414–1451 | Khizr Khan | Post-Timur invasion |
| Lodi | 1451–1526 | Bahlul Lodi | First Afghan dynasty; Ibrahim Lodi defeated at **Panipat (1526)** |

**Memory Hook:** Mnemonic for the 5 dynasties in order: **S–K–T–S–L** (*Slave, Khilji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, Lodi*).

### High-Yield Exam Facts

- The five dynasties in order: SLAVE/Mamluk (1206–90), KHALJI (1290–1320), TUGHLAQ (1320–1414), SAYYID (1414–51), LODI (1451–1526). Mnemonic: “Slaves Keep The Sultan’s Law”.
- Qutb-ud-din AIBAK (1206–10): Ghori’s Turkish slave, governor of his Indian lands, founder of the Slave dynasty; called “Lakh Baksh” (giver of lakhs) for generosity; began the Qutub Minar (named for the sufi Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki); died at Lahore playing chaugan (horse polo). His incapable son Aram Shah lasted eight months.
- ILTUTMISH (1211–36): the real consolidator — completed the Qutub Minar, introduced the silver TANKA and copper JITAL, organized the CHAHALGANI (corps of forty Turkish nobles), and saved India from Chingiz Khan by refusing refuge to the Khwarizm prince (1221). He nominated his daughter RAZIA (1236–40) — the first and only woman on the Delhi throne; her rise fell foul of the Forty.
- BALBAN (1266–87): broke the Chahalgani, ruled by “blood and iron”, enforced SIJDA (prostration) and PAIBOS (kissing the royal feet), introduced the Persian Nauroz festival, ran an efficient spy network, and championed Turkish-only nobility — theory of kingship: the Sultan as Zil-e-Ilahi, shadow of God.
- ALAUDDIN KHALJI (1296–1316): first Sultan with a large PERMANENT standing army paid in cash; introduced DAGH (horse branding) and HULIYA (soldier descriptive rolls); ruthless MARKET CONTROL — fixed prices, separate markets, the shahna-i-mandi inspector; land revenue raised to half the produce in the doab. His general Malik Kafur raided the deep south (Devagiri, Warangal, Madurai).
- MUHAMMAD-BIN-TUGHLAQ (1325–51): the Sultanate’s great experimenter. (1) Capital transfer 1327: Delhi → Devagiri, renamed DAULATABAD, to control the south — the whole population force-marched 1,500+ km; water scarcity forced the return two years later. (2) TOKEN CURRENCY 1329: copper coins valued as silver, on the Chinese paper-money model — forgery exploded, the treasury emptied redeeming them. Brilliant ideas, broken execution.
- FIROZ SHAH TUGHLAQ (1351–88): the builder-welfare Sultan — canals, new towns (Firozabad, Hisar), employment bureau, Diwan-i-Khairat (charity); but he revived the jagir system and made the army hereditary, weakening the centre. After him: TIMUR, 1398 — the Chagatai Mongol sacked Delhi for three days against barely any opposition, and his withdrawal in 1399 was the death blow to the Tughlaqs.
- Endgame: the SAYYIDS (1414–51, Khizr Khan — Timur’s nominee) ruled a shrunken Delhi; the LODIS (Afghan, not Turkish) followed — Bahlol (1451–89), SIKANDAR (1489–1517, founded AGRA 1504, moved the capital there), and IBRAHIM (1517–26), whose harshness pushed Daulat Khan Lodi to invite Babur. First Battle of Panipat, 21 April 1526 — the Sultanate ends where the Gateway-Battles chapter picks up.

chapters.heading: 7. Medieval South: Cholas to Talikota
chapters.body_markdown:
**Overview:** Chola navy on the Kaveri, Vijayanagara on the Tungabhadra, Bahmani rivalry.

**Core Mental Model:** The medieval south runs on rivers: Chola power grew from the Kaveri delta and sailed to the Ganga and Srivijaya; Vijayanagara rose on the Tungabhadra; and the Krishna–Tungabhadra doab was the bleeding frontier with the Bahmani sultans — until Talikota, 1565.

### High-Yield Exam Facts

- The IMPERIAL CHOLAS (c. 850–1200) rebuilt Tamil power from the Kaveri delta. RAJARAJA I (985–1014) conquered Kerala, northern Sri Lanka and the Maldives, and raised the Brihadesvara (Rajarajesvaram) temple at Thanjavur — the grandest Dravidian temple, completed 1010.
- RAJENDRA I (1014–44) took the empire to its peak: marched north and defeated MAHIPALA I of the Pala empire of Bengal, and to commemorate it founded GANGAIKONDACHOLAPURAM (“the Chola who took the Ganga”) with its own Rajesvaram temple. Called Pandita Cholan for his patronage of learning.
- The Chola NAVY was the age’s wonder: the c. 1025 expedition against SRIVIJAYA (Malaya–Sumatra) secured the eastern sea lanes to China. Chola local government is equally famous — the Uttaramerur inscriptions describe elected village assemblies (sabha/ur) with committee (variyam) systems.
- VIJAYANAGARA (1336–1672): founded by HARIHARA and BUKKA of the Sangama dynasty on the Tungabhadra — capital HAMPI. Four dynasties: Sangama → Saluva → Tuluva → Aravidu. Deva Raya II (1425–46) recruited Muslim cavalry and archers to modernize the army.
- The BAHMANI kingdom (1347–1527): founded by ALAUDDIN HASAN BAHMAN SHAH in revolt against Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq; capital first at GULBARGA, later BIDAR. Its greatest figure was the minister MAHMUD GAWAN (1461–81) — conquests, administrative reform, and the great madrasa at Bidar — executed on a forged letter; the kingdom then split into the five Deccan sultanates (Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golkonda, Bidar, Berar).
- Vijayanagara vs Bahmani: a 200-year war over the RAICHUR DOAB — the fertile, fort-studded strip between the Krishna and the Tungabhadra. KRISHNADEVA RAYA (1509–29, Tuluva) was the climax: took Raichur (1520), patronized Telugu letters (Amuktamalyada), hosted Portuguese travellers (Domingo Paes) — the “Andhra Bhoja”.
- TALIKOTA (Rakshasa-Tangadi / Bannihatti), 1565: the combined Deccan sultanates — Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golkonda and Bidar (all except Berar) — crushed Vijayanagara; regent RAMA RAYA was captured and executed, Hampi sacked. The empire lingered under the Aravidus but the south’s balance of power was broken — setting the stage for the Mughals and then the Europeans.

chapters.heading: 8. Europeans: Ports to Power
chapters.body_markdown:
**Overview:** Five flags, one coastline — settlements, Carnatic, Mysore & Maratha wars.

**Core Mental Model:** Five European flags on one coastline. Learn each power’s port pairs — Portuguese–Goa, Dutch–Pulicat, English–Madras/Bombay/Calcutta, French–Pondicherry, Danes–Tranquebar — and the wars of conquest are just those ports fighting their way inland.

### High-Yield Exam Facts

- PORTUGUESE: Vasco da Gama reached CALICUT in 1498 (welcomed by the Zamorin, resented by Arab traders); returned 1501. Almeida (Governor 1505) pushed the BLUE WATER POLICY — mastery of the Indian Ocean; ALBUQUERQUE took GOA from Bijapur in 1510 (the first European-held Indian territory since Alexander); Nino da Cunha moved HQ Cochin→Goa in 1530. They brought tobacco cultivation and India’s first printing press (Goa, 1556).
- DUTCH: the VOC formed 1602; Masulipatnam 1605, PULICAT 1610, Surat 1616, Cochin 1663 — spice-focused, and eventually squeezed out (Battle of Bedara vs the English, 1759). DANES: company founded 1616; TRANQUEBAR (1620) near Tanjore and SERAMPORE near Calcutta — remembered for missionaries more than trade; sold out to Britain in 1845.
- ENGLISH: Charter from Elizabeth I on 31 December 1600 to the “Governor and Company of Merchants of London trading into the East Indies”. Battle of Surat 1612 beat the Portuguese at sea → Jahangir allowed the SURAT factory (1613); Sir THOMAS ROE (1615) at Jahangir’s court as James I’s ambassador. Madras/Fort St. George 1639–40; BOMBAY came as Portuguese dowry to Charles II (1662) → Company 1668 → HQ 1687; JOB CHARNOCK’s Sutanati treaty 1690 → zamindari of Sutanati, Govindpur, Kalikata (1698) → FORT WILLIAM 1700 = Calcutta.
- FRENCH: Colbert’s Compagnie des Indes Orientales, 1664, under Louis XIV; PONDICHERRY founded 1674 — the nerve centre; reorganized 1720 as the Perpetual Company, strengthened under Lenoir and Dumas, weaponized under DUPLEIX.
- CARNATIC WARS — the Anglo-French duel: 1st (1746–48): French take Madras; Battle of ST. THOME — Dupleix’s small French force routs the Carnatic Nawab’s army; Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (Austrian Succession in the background). 2nd (1749–54): puppet politics — French back Muzaffar Jung (Hyderabad) + Chanda Sahib (Carnatic), English back Nasir Jung + Muhammad Ali; Clive’s side wins; Treaty of Pondicherry/Godehu 1754. 3rd (1756–63): Lally takes Fort St. David but is crushed at WANDIWASH (1760, Eyre Coote); Treaty of Paris 1763 returns Pondicherry as a trading post — French political power in India is finished.
- ANGLO-MYSORE WARS: 1st (1767–69) — HAIDAR ALI beats the English; Treaty of Madras. 2nd (1780–84) — Treaty of Mangalore under Warren Hastings. 3rd (1790–92) — Cornwallis vs TIPU; Treaty of Srirangapatna halves Mysore. 4th (1799) — Wellesley storms SRIRANGAPATNA; Tipu dies fighting. Mysore falls to Subsidiary Alliance.
- ANGLO-MARATHA WARS: 1st (1775–82) — English humiliated at WADGAON (Convention of Wadgaon, 1779), then Treaty of SALBAI (1782) abandoning Raghunath Rao. 2nd (1803–05) — after the Peshwa’s Subsidiary Alliance Treaty of BASSEIN (1802), the Marathas are beaten; Treaty of Rajghat with the Holkars (1805). 3rd (1817–19) — fought around Lord Hastings’ PINDARI campaign; Maratha power extinguished, British paramountcy complete.

chapters.heading: 9. Battle of Plassey, 1757
chapters.body_markdown:
**Overview:** How one afternoon on a Bengal riverbank changed who ruled India for two centuries.

**Core Mental Model:** Plassey was a small skirmish that decided two centuries of Indian history — and it was decided by geography, weather, and betrayal, not by numerical strength.

### High-Yield Exam Facts

- By 1757 the Mughal Empire was collapsing. Bengal was its wealthiest province, governed by a semi-independent Nawab.
- The East India Company’s Fort William at Calcutta had become rich on Bengal trade — and had been fortifying without the Nawab’s permission.
- In June 1756 the young Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah seized Calcutta. Surviving prisoners died in a packed cell — the "Black Hole" incident gave the British their pretext.
- Robert Clive sailed from Madras, retook Calcutta, captured the French post of Chandernagore, then marched north with about 3,000 men.
- The Nawab’s army was around 50,000 strong with 50 French-officered cannons. The British were outnumbered roughly 17 to 1.
- But Clive had bribed Mir Jafar, the Nawab’s commander, with the throne. A third of Bengal’s army would not fight.
- During the battle a sudden monsoon downpour soaked the Nawab’s gunpowder. The British had covered theirs with tarpaulins. The artillery duel was decided by weather.
- Within three hours the Nawab’s army broke. Mir Jafar was installed as the puppet Nawab.
- By 1765 the Company held the Diwani — the right to collect revenue — of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa. Merchants had become rulers.

chapters.heading: 10. Freedom Struggle on the Map
chapters.body_markdown:
**Overview:** 1857 centres & leaders; Champaran to Dandi to Quit India.

**Core Mental Model:** Two map-layers of resistance: 1857’s garrison towns each paired with a leader, and Gandhi’s satyagrahas each pinned to a village. Centre–leader and movement–place pairings are what exams actually test.

### Revolt of 1857 — Centres & Leaders

| Centre | Indian Leader(s) | British Suppressor |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Delhi | Bahadur Shah II & Bakht Khan | John Nicholson |
| **Kanpur** | **Nana Saheb** & Tantia Tope | Sir Colin Campbell |
| Lucknow | Begum Hazrat Mahal | Sir Colin Campbell |
| Jhansi | Rani Lakshmibai | Sir Hugh Rose |
| Bihar (Jagdishpur) | Kunwar Singh | William Taylor |

**Exam Trap:** **Swadeshi & Boycott** were first adopted as mass-struggle methods during the **1905 Partition of Bengal** (Lord Curzon) — NOT the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920). **Calcutta** remained British India’s capital until **1911**.

### High-Yield Exam Facts

- 1857 causes: Awadh annexed (1856) for “maladministration”, Jhansi via Doctrine of Lapse (Dalhousie, 1848–56: no adopted heir allowed); sepoy grievances (low pay, ceiling at subedar, racial discrimination); social reforms + missionaries; economic drain. Immediate spark: the Enfield cartridge greased with cow and pig fat.
- Sequence: 19th NI at Berhampur refuses the cartridge → Mangal Pandey (34th NI) fires at his sergeant-major at Barrackpore and is hanged → the revolt proper breaks out at MEERUT on 10 May 1857 → sepoys reach Delhi and declare Bahadur Shah Zafar Emperor of India.
- Centre → leader pairs (learn as a table): Delhi – Bahadur Shah II + Gen. Bakht Khan; Lucknow – Begum Hazrat Mahal; Kanpur – Nana Sahib with Tantia Tope & Azimullah Khan; Jhansi – Rani Laxmibai; Bareilly – Khan Bahadur; Allahabad – Liaqat Ali; Jagdishpur/Arrah – Kunwar Singh; Faizabad – Maulvi Ahmadullah.
- Consequence: Government of India Act 1858 abolished Company rule — the Crown ruled directly. (Also remember Wellesley’s Subsidiary Alliance and Dalhousie’s Doctrine of Lapse as the annexation machinery that fed the revolt.)
- Gandhi’s laboratory: Champaran 1917 = FIRST civil disobedience (indigo planters’ tinkathia); Kheda 1918 = FIRST non-cooperation (crop failure → revenue withheld under the revenue code). Then Jallianwala Bagh (13 Apr 1919) and Khilafat fed into the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22), financed by the Tilak Swarajya Fund.
- Chauri Chaura, February 1922: a mob burnt a police station; Gandhi withdrew the Non-Cooperation Movement at its height — the most argued-about decision of the era, and the cause of the Swarajist split.
- Civil Disobedience began 12 March 1930: Gandhi + 78 chosen followers walked ~375 km from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi on the Gujarat seacoast and broke the salt law on 6 April. Salt was genius: the one tax every villager paid.
- Quit India: the AICC met at Bombay on 8 August 1942 and passed the resolution — “Do or Die”. Leadership was jailed within hours; the movement went leaderless and underground. Gandhi fasted 21 days (Feb–Mar 1943) against the repression.

chapters.heading: 11. Modern India Milestones, Mizoram History & World History
chapters.body_markdown:
**Overview:** High-frequency MPSC Prelims & Clerical anchors covering Mughal culture, 1857, INC, the Gandhian Era, Mizoram’s political journey, and World History turning points.

**Core Mental Model:** Link every modern Indian event to its decade anchor — 1857 (Revolt), 1885 (INC), 1905 (Swadeshi), 1911 (Delhi capital), 1920/1930/1942 (Gandhi’s three mass movements) — and pair Mizoram’s journey from 1894 (Alphabet) to 1986 (Peace Accord) & 1987 (Statehood).

### Mizoram History Chronology (1871–1987)

| Year | Milestone |
| --- | --- |
| 1871–72 & 1889–90 | First & Second Lushai Expeditions; British administration begins |
| 11 Jan 1894 | J.H. Lorrain (*Pu Buanga*) & F.W. Savidge (*Sap Upa*) arrive; Mizo alphabet created |
| 1946 / 1952 | Mizo Union founded (1946); Lushai Hills Autonomous District Council (1952) |
| 1954 / 1959 | Abolition of Chieftainship (1954); Mautam bamboo-flowering famine (1959) |
| 1972 | Mizoram becomes a Union Territory (LADC, MADC, CADC created) |
| 30 Jun 1986 | **Mizoram Peace Accord** signed (GoI + MNF) |
| 20 Feb 1987 | **23rd State of India** inaugurated with Art. 371G protection |

### High-Frequency Indian History Anchors

- **Vedic & Classical:** Six Vedangas are *Shiksha, Kalpa, Vyakarana, Nirukta, Chhanda, Jyotisha*. Akbar introduced **Din-i-Ilahi** (1582) as a syncretic ethical order.
- **Indian National Congress (1885):** Founded by A.O. Hume in Bombay; first President was **W.C. Bonnerjee** (72 delegates).
- **Partition of Bengal (1905):** Lord Curzon partitioned Bengal; **Swadeshi & Boycott** were adopted as mass struggle methods for the first time during this agitation.
- **Capital Shift (1911):** Calcutta remained the capital of British India until **1911**, when the Delhi Durbar announced the shift to New Delhi.
- **Gandhian Mass Movements:** Champaran (1917) → Kheda & Ahmedabad (1918) → Non-Cooperation (1920–22) → Civil Disobedience / Dandi March (1930) → Quit India (August 1942).

### World History Quick Landmarks

- **1776:** American Declaration of Independence · **1789:** French Revolution (*Liberty, Equality, Fraternity*) · **1914–1918:** World War I (Treaty of Versailles, 1919) · **1917:** Russian Revolution · **1939–1945:** World War II → **United Nations founded (24 October 1945)**.

title: Computer & IT Fundamentals
summary: 5 exam-ready chapters covering Hardware/Memory, Windows Shortcuts & OS, MS Word/Excel/PowerPoint, OSI Networking & Cybersecurity, and DBMS/SQL — tuned for 7,450+ Computer & IT PYQs.

chapters.heading: 1. Hardware, CPU, Memory Hierarchy & Binary Units
chapters.body_markdown:
**Core Mental Model:** A computer processes data in four stages (Input → Processing → Output → Storage). Speed increases and capacity shrinks as you move closer to the CPU: **Registers > L1/L2/L3 Cache > RAM > SSD/HDD**.

### Memory Types Comparison

| Memory | Volatility | Speed | Primary Role |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CPU Registers | Volatile | Fastest | Holds immediate ALU operands & instruction pointer |
| Cache (SRAM) | Volatile | Very fast | Bridges CPU–RAM speed gap (flip-flops, no refresh needed) |
| RAM (DRAM) | Volatile | Fast | Holds active OS & running apps; loses data on power-off |
| ROM / BIOS / UEFI | Non-volatile | Moderate | Stores boot firmware (POST — Power-On Self-Test) |
| SSD / HDD / Optical | Non-volatile | Slower | Permanent mass storage (flash vs magnetic platters) |

### Binary & Storage Units

| Unit | Exact Value | Quick Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 Nibble | 4 bits | 1 hexadecimal digit |
| 1 Byte | 8 bits | 1 ASCII character (256 values) |
| 1 KB | 1,024 Bytes (2¹⁰) | Kilobyte |
| 1 MB | 1,024 KB (2²⁰ B) | Megabyte |
| 1 GB | 1,024 MB (2³⁰ B) | Gigabyte |
| 1 TB | 1,024 GB (2⁴⁰ B) | Terabyte |

- **CPU components:** ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit), CU (Control Unit — fetches/decodes), and Registers.
- **Computer Generations:** 1st Vacuum Tubes → 2nd Transistors → 3rd Integrated Circuits (IC) → 4th Microprocessors (VLSI) → 5th AI / ULSI.
- **Input vs Output:** OCR, OMR, MICR (cheques), Barcode Reader, Joystick = Input; Plotter, Laser Printer, Monitor, Speaker = Output.

**Exam Trap:** **RAM is volatile** (clears when power turns off) — that is why it cannot be used for permanent storage. **SRAM** is faster and costlier than **DRAM** and is used in Cache, whereas DRAM is used in main RAM.

chapters.heading: 2. Operating Systems, File Systems & Windows Shortcuts
chapters.body_markdown:
**Core Mental Model:** The Operating System (OS) is the resource manager sitting between hardware and user applications — handling **process scheduling, memory management (paging/virtual memory), file systems, and device drivers**.

### High-Frequency Windows Shortcuts

| Shortcut | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `Alt + Tab` | Switch between open applications |
| `Win + D` | Show / hide Desktop (minimise all windows) |
| `Win + L` | Lock the computer |
| `Ctrl + Shift + Esc` | Open Task Manager directly |
| `Alt + F4` | Close active window / Shut down on Desktop |
| `Shift + Delete` | Permanently delete file (bypasses Recycle Bin) |
| `F2` | Rename selected file or folder |
| `Win + E` | Open File Explorer |

- **Booting:** Cold boot (power from off) vs Warm boot (restart via `Ctrl+Alt+Del` or Restart).
- **OS Types:** Batch, Time-sharing, Real-Time (RTOS — missiles/medical), Distributed, Embedded.
- **Deadlock Conditions (Coffman):** Mutual Exclusion, Hold & Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait.
- **File Extensions:** `.exe` (executable), `.pdf` (Portable Document Format), `.csv` (comma-separated values), `.zip` (compressed archive).

**Exam Trap:** `Ctrl + Shift + Esc` opens **Task Manager** directly, whereas `Ctrl + Alt + Del` opens the Windows Security screen first. **Thrashing** occurs when a system spends more time swapping pages (virtual memory) than executing instructions.

chapters.heading: 3. MS Office — Word, Excel Formulas & PowerPoint
chapters.body_markdown:
**Core Mental Model:** MPSC & MSSSB Computer papers test practical office fluency — knowing **which tool solves a formatting/data task** and exact keyboard shortcuts.

### MS Word, Excel & PowerPoint Essentials

| Application | Feature / Shortcut | What It Does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MS Word | **Format Painter** (`Ctrl+Shift+C` / `V`) | Copies exact text/paragraph formatting to another selection |
| MS Word | **Mail Merge** | Combines a template letter with a recipient data source (Excel/CSV) |
| MS Word | `Ctrl + H` / `Ctrl + K` / `F7` | Find & Replace / Insert Hyperlink / Spelling & Grammar check |
| MS Word | `Ctrl + J` / `Ctrl + E` | Justify align / Center align |
| MS Excel | `$A$1` (Absolute Reference) | Locks both column and row when copying formulas (`F4` toggles) |
| MS Excel | `=SUM()`, `=AVERAGE()`, `=COUNT()`, `=IF()` | Core aggregation & conditional formulas (always begin with `=`) |
| MS PowerPoint | `F5` / `Shift + F5` | Start slideshow from slide 1 / from current slide |
| MS PowerPoint | `Ctrl + M` vs `Ctrl + N` | Insert **new slide** vs open **new presentation** |

**Exam Trap:** In PowerPoint, `Ctrl + M` inserts a **new slide** inside the current deck, while `Ctrl + N` creates an entirely new presentation. In Word, **Gutter margin** adds extra space on the binding side for printing/bookbinding. Default modern extensions: `.docx`, `.xlsx`, `.pptx`.

chapters.heading: 4. Computer Networks, OSI/TCP-IP, Internet & Cybersecurity
chapters.body_markdown:
**Core Mental Model:** Data travels down the sender’s **7-layer OSI stack** (encapsulation) and up the receiver’s stack. Knowing **which device & protocol sits at which layer** solves most networking questions.

### OSI 7 Layers, Devices & Protocols

| Layer | Name | Key Device / Protocol |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 7 | Application | HTTP (80), HTTPS (443), FTP (21), SMTP (25), DNS (53), POP3/IMAP |
| 6 | Presentation | SSL/TLS encryption, compression (JPEG, ASCII) |
| 5 | Session | Session setup, checkpointing, NetBIOS |
| 4 | Transport | **TCP** (reliable, connection-oriented) & **UDP** (fast, connectionless) |
| 3 | Network | **Router**, IP (IPv4 = 32-bit, IPv6 = 128-bit), ICMP (`ping`) |
| 2 | Data Link | **Switch**, Bridge, MAC address (48-bit), Ethernet Frames |
| 1 | Physical | **Hub**, Repeater, Cables (Twisted Pair, Fiber Optic), Bits |

**Memory Hook:** OSI Layers bottom-to-top (1→7): **P**lease **D**o **N**ot **T**hrow **S**ausage **P**izza **A**way (Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application).

- **Topologies:** Star (central switch — most common LAN), Bus (single backbone), Ring, Mesh (highest fault tolerance).
- **Cybersecurity:** **Phishing** (fake emails/sites stealing credentials), **Ransomware** (encrypts files for ransom), **Trojan** (disguised legitimate software), **Firewall** (filters network traffic), **HTTPS** (HTTP over TLS/SSL).

**Exam Trap:** **SMTP** *sends* email (outgoing); **POP3 / IMAP** *receives* email (incoming). **DNS** translates domain names (`study.hawayu.in`) into IP addresses. **Switch** works at Layer 2 (MAC), **Router** at Layer 3 (IP), and **Hub** at Layer 1 (broadcasts to all ports).

chapters.heading: 5. Databases, Keys, Normalization & SQL Basics
chapters.body_markdown:
**Core Mental Model:** A Relational DBMS (RDBMS) stores data in tables (**relations**) of rows (**tuples**) and columns (**attributes**), linked via keys and protected by **ACID** transactions.

### Database Keys & SQL Command Groups

| Concept | Meaning & Exam Example |
| --- | --- |
| Primary Key | Uniquely identifies every row; **cannot be NULL** or duplicate |
| Foreign Key | Column referencing the Primary Key of another table (referential integrity) |
| Candidate / Super Key | Minimal unique identifier / any superset of a candidate key |
| DDL (Structure) | `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE` |
| DML (Data) | `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` |
| DCL / TCL | `GRANT`, `REVOKE` / `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`, `SAVEPOINT` |

- **ACID Properties:** **A**tomicity (all-or-nothing), **C**onsistency, **I**solation, **D**urability.
- **Normalization:** 1NF (atomic values, no repeating groups) → 2NF (no partial dependency) → 3NF (no transitive dependency) → BCNF.

**Exam Trap:** `DELETE` removes specific rows (can use `WHERE` and be rolled back); `TRUNCATE` removes all rows fast and resets identity; `DROP` deletes the entire table structure itself.

title: General Science Essentials
summary: 4 high-yield chapters covering Physics (SI units, optics, electricity), Chemistry (formulas, alloys, acids), Biology (vitamins, hormones, diseases), and ISRO/Space — linked to 1,572+ Science PYQs.

chapters.heading: 1. Physics — SI Units, Mechanics, Optics, Heat & Electricity
chapters.body_markdown:
**Core Mental Model:** Competitive Physics questions test **everyday applications of laws** (why the sky is blue, which mirror goes in headlights vs rear-view, Ohm’s law, SI units, and wave properties).

### High-Yield SI Units & Instruments

| Quantity | SI Unit | Measuring Instrument |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Force / Weight | Newton (N) | Spring balance |
| Pressure | Pascal (Pa = N/m²) | Barometer (air), Manometer (gas) |
| Work / Energy / Heat | Joule (J) | Calorimeter (heat) |
| Power | Watt (W = J/s) | 1 Horsepower (HP) = **746 W** |
| Electric Current / Resistance | Ampere (A) / Ohm (Ω) | Ammeter (series) / Voltmeter (parallel) |
| Frequency / Sound Loudness | Hertz (Hz) / Decibel (dB) | Audiometer / Sonar (ultrasound) |
| Optical Power of Lens | Dioptre (`P = 1/f` in m) | Convex (+), Concave (−) |

### Mirrors, Lenses & Eye Defects

| Application / Defect | Mirror or Lens Used | Key Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vehicle rear-view mirror | **Convex mirror** | Always erect, diminished, wider field of view |
| Headlights, shaving & dentist mirror | **Concave mirror** | Parallel beam / magnified erect image up close |
| Myopia (near-sightedness) | **Concave lens** | Image forms in front of retina; diverges rays |
| Hypermetropia (far-sightedness) | **Convex lens** | Image forms behind retina; converges rays |
| Astigmatism | **Cylindrical lens** | Uneven corneal curvature |

- **Light Phenomena:** Sky blue & sunset red = **Rayleigh Scattering**; Mirage, Optical Fibre & Diamond sparkle = **Total Internal Reflection (TIR)**; Rainbow = Dispersion + Refraction + Internal Reflection.
- **Thermodynamics:** Specific heat of a gas in an **isothermal** process (ΔT = 0) is **infinity (∞)**; in an **adiabatic** process (ΔQ = 0) it is **zero**.
- **Electricity:** Fuse wire = low melting point, high resistance (lead-tin alloy, placed in **series** on live wire). Household wiring is always in **parallel**.

**Exam Trap:** **Light-year** and **Parsec** are units of **distance** (not time!). Sound waves are **longitudinal mechanical waves** (cannot travel in vacuum; fastest in **solids**, slowest in gases), while light is a **transverse electromagnetic wave** (fastest in vacuum).

chapters.heading: 2. Chemistry — Atomic Structure, Periodic Table, Acids/Bases & Everyday Chemistry
chapters.body_markdown:
**Core Mental Model:** General Chemistry MCQs focus on **common chemical names, pH & acids, alloys, allotropes of carbon, gases, and periodic trends**.

### Must-Know Common Chemicals & Formulas

| Common Name | Chemical Name | Formula | Everyday Use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Baking Soda | Sodium bicarbonate | `NaHCO₃` | Antacid, baking, fire extinguisher |
| Washing Soda | Sodium carbonate decahydrate | `Na₂CO₃·10H₂O` | Softening hard water, detergent |
| Bleaching Powder | Calcium oxychloride | `CaOCl₂` | Water disinfection, bleaching |
| Plaster of Paris | Calcium sulphate hemihydrate | `CaSO₄·½H₂O` | Casts, moulds (from Gypsum `2H₂O`) |
| Laughing Gas | Nitrous oxide | `N₂O` | Mild anaesthetic |
| Dry Ice | Solid carbon dioxide | `CO₂(s)` | Sublimation cooling |
| Quick Lime / Slaked Lime | Calcium oxide / hydroxide | `CaO` / `Ca(OH)₂` | Cement / whitewashing |

### Key Alloys & Everyday Acids

| Alloy / Source | Composition / Acid |
| --- | --- |
| Brass / Bronze | Copper + Zinc (**Brass**) / Copper + Tin (**Bronze**) |
| Solder / Stainless Steel | Lead + Tin / Iron + Chromium + Nickel + Carbon |
| Vinegar / Lemon / Tamarind / Ant sting | Acetic / Citric / Tartaric / **Formic (Methanoic)** acid |
| Curd / Stomach gastric juice / Car battery | Lactic / **Hydrochloric (HCl)** / **Sulphuric (H₂SO₄)** acid |

- **Allotropes of Carbon:** **Graphite** (used in pencils & lubricants; good conductor of electricity), **Diamond** (hardest natural substance; electrical insulator), Fullerene (C₆₀).
- **pH Scale (0–14):** `< 7` Acidic, `= 7` Neutral (pure water), `> 7` Basic. Human blood pH = **7.35–7.45** (slightly alkaline).
- **Isotopes vs Isobars:** Isotopes = same atomic number (protons), different mass number (e.g., ¹²C, ¹⁴C); Isobars = same mass number, different atomic number.

**Exam Trap:** **Aqua Regia** (dissolves gold & platinum) is a **3 : 1** mixture of concentrated **HCl** and concentrated **HNO₃**. **Graphite** (not lead!) is used in pencil leads. **Mercury** is the only liquid metal; **Bromine** is the only liquid non-metal at room temperature.

chapters.heading: 3. Biology — Cells, Human Body Systems, Hormones, Vitamins & Diseases
chapters.body_markdown:
**Core Mental Model:** Biology in MPSC/MSSSB revolves around **cell organelles, endocrine hormones, blood groups, vitamin deficiencies, and pathogen classification (viral vs bacterial vs protozoan)**.

### Vitamins & Deficiency Diseases

| Vitamin | Chemical Name | Solubility | Deficiency Disease |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Vitamin A | Retinol | Fat (A, D, E, K) | Night blindness, Xerophthalmia |
| Vitamin B₁ | Thiamine | Water (B, C) | Beri-beri |
| Vitamin B₃ / B₁₂ | Niacin / Cobalamin | Water | Pellagra / Pernicious anaemia (contains Cobalt) |
| Vitamin C | Ascorbic acid | Water | Scurvy (bleeding gums) |
| Vitamin D | Calciferol | Fat | Rickets (children), Osteomalacia (adults) |
| Vitamin K | Phylloquinone | Fat | Delayed blood clotting |

### Endocrine Glands & Hormones

| Gland | Hormone | Core Function / Disorder |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pituitary (“Master Gland”) | Growth Hormone (GH), TSH | Controls other glands; Dwarfism / Gigantism |
| Thyroid | Thyroxine (needs Iodine) | Metabolism; deficiency causes **Goitre** |
| Pancreas (Islets of Langerhans) | **Insulin** (Beta cells) / Glucagon (Alpha) | Lowers / raises blood sugar (**Diabetes mellitus**) |
| Adrenal | Adrenaline | Fight-or-flight emergency hormone |

- **Cell Organelles:** Mitochondria = powerhouse (ATP); Ribosomes = protein synthesis (built from **amino acids**); Lysosomes = suicidal bags; Chloroplast = photosynthesis (plants).
- **Blood:** Universal Donor = **O−** (O); Universal Recipient = **AB+** (AB); Red colour = Haemoglobin (Iron); Clotting = Platelets + Fibrinogen + Vitamin K.
- **Pathogens:** Viral (Polio, Dengue, AIDS, Rabies, Measles, COVID-19); Bacterial (TB, Typhoid, Cholera, Tetanus, Leprosy); Protozoan (Malaria — *Plasmodium* via female *Anopheles*, Kala-azar, Amoebiasis).

**Exam Trap:** **Beta cells** of the Islets of Langerhans in the pancreas secrete **Insulin** (which *lowers* blood glucose), while Alpha cells secrete Glucagon. **Bile** is produced by the **Liver** (largest gland) and stored in the Gall Bladder — it emulsifies fats but contains **no digestive enzymes**.

chapters.heading: 4. Space (ISRO PSLV/GSLV), Defence & Applied Science
chapters.body_markdown:
**Core Mental Model:** ISRO & Science-in-the-News questions test **launch vehicles (PSLV vs GSLV/LVM3), orbits (LEO vs GEO), landmark Indian missions, and nuclear/biotech basics**.

### ISRO Launch Vehicles Compared

| Vehicle | Stages & Fuel | Target Orbit & Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **PSLV** (Workhorse) | 4 stages (Solid–Liquid–Solid–Liquid) | Sun-Synchronous Polar Orbit (SSPO) — remote sensing, Chandrayaan-1, Mangalyaan, Aditya-L1 |
| **GSLV Mk-II** | 3 stages (Solid–Liquid–**Cryogenic** LOX/LH₂) | Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO) — heavier communication satellites (~2.2 tonnes) |
| **LVM3** (formerly GSLV Mk-III) | 3 stages (2 solid S200 + L110 liquid + C25 cryogenic) | Heavy-lift (~4 tonnes GTO) — Chandrayaan-2, Chandrayaan-3, Gaganyaan |

- **Key ISRO Centres:** HQ = Bengaluru; Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC) = Thiruvananthapuram; Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC) = **Sriharikota** (Andhra Pradesh, launchpad).
- **Landmark Missions:** Aryabhata (1975, first Indian satellite), Chandrayaan-1 (2008, lunar water), Mangalyaan / MOM (2013, first Asian Mars orbiter), Chandrayaan-3 (Aug 2023, lunar south pole soft landing — *Shiv Shakti* point), Aditya-L1 (Sun–Earth L1 point).
- **Nuclear Energy:** Fission (splitting heavy U-235/Pu-239 in reactors; Heavy Water `D₂O` or Graphite = moderator, Cadmium/Boron = control rods) vs Fusion (combining light H nuclei — powers the Sun & stars).

**Exam Trap:** The core difference between **PSLV** and **GSLV** is **payload capacity + target orbit + cryogenic upper stage** (PSLV has 4 alternating solid/liquid stages for polar orbits; GSLV uses a 3rd-stage **cryogenic engine** to push heavier communication satellites to GTO).

title: Indian Economy & Banking
summary: 5 focused Economy chapters — National Income/GDP, RBI Monetary Policy & MUDRA, Budget Deficits & GST, Unemployment/Inflation/NITI Aayog, and Balance of Payments — mapped to 677+ Economy PYQs.

chapters.heading: 1. National Income, GDP/GNP & Sectors of the Economy
chapters.body_markdown:
**Core Mental Model:** **Domestic (GDP)** cares about *geography* (produced inside India’s borders regardless of nationality); **National (GNP)** cares about *citizenship* (produced by Indian residents anywhere in the world).

### Core National Income Identities

| Formula | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `GNP = GDP + NFIA` | Add Net Factor Income from Abroad |
| `NDP = GDP − Depreciation` | Net = Gross minus Wear & Tear |
| `NNP (at Factor Cost) = National Income` | NNP at Market Price − Indirect Taxes + Subsidies |
| `Per Capita Income = National Income ÷ Population` | Average income per citizen |
| `Real GDP = Nominal GDP ÷ (GDP Deflator / 100)` | Adjusted for inflation (base year prices) |

- **Three Sectors:** **Primary** (Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing, Mining — largest employer in India), **Secondary** (Manufacturing, Construction, Utilities), **Tertiary / Services** (IT, Banking, Trade, Transport — **largest contributor to India’s GDP**, >50%).
- **Official Agency:** National Statistical Office (**NSO**, under MoSPI — formed by merging CSO & NSSO) estimates India’s GDP.

**Exam Trap:** **Real GDP** (constant base-year prices) measures true volume growth, whereas **Nominal GDP** includes price inflation. Transfer payments (pensions, scholarships, unemployment dole) are **excluded** from National Income because no current good/service is produced.

chapters.heading: 2. Money, Banking, RBI Monetary Policy & Financial Schemes
chapters.body_markdown:
**Core Mental Model:** The **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** — established 1 April 1935 (Hilton Young Commission), nationalised 1 Jan 1949 — controls inflation and liquidity via **Quantitative** (economy-wide) and **Qualitative** (sector-specific) credit control tools.

### RBI Monetary Policy Instruments

| Instrument | Mechanism | Effect When Raised (Hawkish) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Repo Rate** | Rate at which banks borrow short-term from RBI against govt securities | Borrowing costlier → curbs inflation |
| **Reverse Repo / SDF** | Rate at which RBI absorbs surplus liquidity from banks | Banks park cash with RBI → reduces money supply |
| **CRR** (Cash Reserve Ratio) | % of NDTL kept as **cash** with RBI (earns 0% interest) | Reduces lendable funds |
| **SLR** (Statutory Liquidity Ratio) | % of NDTL kept by banks in liquid assets (cash, gold, G-Secs) | Restricts commercial lending |
| **Bank Rate** | Long-term discount/penalty rate without collateral | Signals dear money |
| **OMO** (Open Market Operations) | RBI buys/sells Govt securities in open market | Selling G-Secs sucks out liquidity |

### Flagship Financial Inclusion Schemes

| Scheme | Key Exam Facts |
| --- | --- |
| **PM MUDRA Yojana (PMMY)** | Collateral-free micro-enterprise loans: **Shishu** (up to ₹50,000), **Kishor** (₹50,001–₹5 lakh), **Tarun** (₹5 lakh–₹10 lakh; Tarun Plus up to ₹20 lakh) |
| **PM Jan Dhan Yojana (2014)** | Zero-balance bank accounts, RuPay debit card, overdraft facility |
| **NABARD (1982)** | Apex rural & agricultural credit institution (Sivaraman Committee) |
| **SEBI (1988; statutory 1992)** | Capital market & stock exchange regulator |

**Exam Trap:** **Taxation and Government Expenditure** are **Fiscal Policy** tools (Ministry of Finance), **NOT** RBI credit-control instruments! The **Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)** has **6 members** (3 RBI + 3 Govt), chaired by the RBI Governor, targeting CPI inflation at **4% ± 2%**.

chapters.heading: 3. Union Budget, Fiscal Deficits, GST & Taxation
chapters.body_markdown:
**Core Mental Model:** Under **Art. 112**, the Union Budget (“Annual Financial Statement”) splits into **Revenue Account** (day-to-day income & expenses that don’t change assets/liabilities) and **Capital Account** (loans, borrowings, disinvestment, and asset creation like highways).

### Budget Deficits & Tax Classification

| Term | Exact Formula / Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Revenue Deficit** | Revenue Expenditure − Revenue Receipts |
| **Fiscal Deficit** | Total Expenditure − (Revenue Receipts + Non-Debt Capital Receipts) = **Total Borrowing** |
| **Primary Deficit** | **Fiscal Deficit − Interest Payments** (current-year borrowing excluding past debt interest) |
| **Direct Taxes** | Burden cannot be shifted: **Income Tax**, Corporate Tax, Capital Gains Tax |
| **Indirect Taxes** | Burden shifted to consumer: **GST** (101st Amendment, 1 July 2017), **Customs Duty** (export/import) |

- **GST Council (Art. 279A):** Chaired by the Union Finance Minister; Centre has 1/3rd voting weight, States 2/3rd; decisions require 3/4th majority.
- **Finance Commission (Art. 280):** Constitutional body constituted every 5 years by the President to recommend Centre–State tax devolution (16th FC chaired by Dr. Arvind Panagariya).

**Exam Trap:** **Customs Duty** is the tax imposed on the **import and export of commodities**. **GST** subsumed VAT, Excise, and Service Tax, but **petroleum products and alcohol for human consumption** remain outside GST.

chapters.heading: 4. Inflation, Unemployment, Poverty & Planning (NITI Aayog)
chapters.body_markdown:
**Core Mental Model:** Distinguishing the **type of unemployment**, **type of inflation**, and **milestone Five-Year Plans** answers a huge share of GS Economy MCQs.

### Types of Unemployment & Inflation

| Type | Classic Exam Definition |
| --- | --- |
| **Disguised Unemployment** | More workers employed than needed (**marginal productivity = 0**) — classic feature of **Indian agriculture** |
| **Seasonal Unemployment** | Work available only during specific seasons (sowing/harvesting, tourism) |
| **Structural Unemployment** | Skill mismatch between workers and modern job requirements |
| **Frictional Unemployment** | Temporary gap while switching between jobs |
| **Demand-Pull vs Cost-Push** | Too much money chasing too few goods vs rising input/wage costs |
| **Stagflation** | Stagnant growth + high unemployment + high inflation together |

- **CPI vs WPI:** **CPI** (Consumer Price Index, NSO) covers **goods + services** at retail level (RBI’s policy anchor); **WPI** (Wholesale Price Index, DPIIT) covers **only goods** (no services).
- **Planning Milestones:** 1st FYP (1951–56, Harrod–Domar, agriculture); 2nd FYP (1956–61, **Mahalanobis**, heavy industry); 5th FYP (*Garibi Hatao*); **1991 LPG Reforms** (Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation — PV Narasimha Rao & Dr. Manmohan Singh); **NITI Aayog** replaced Planning Commission on **1 Jan 2015** (PM = ex-officio Chairman).
- **Inequality:** **Lorenz Curve** plots income distribution; **Gini Coefficient** (0 = perfect equality, 1 = total inequality) measures it.

**Exam Trap:** **Disguised unemployment** (zero marginal productivity of extra hands on a family farm) is the hallmark of Indian agriculture. **NITI Aayog** is a **non-constitutional, non-statutory** policy think-tank — it does *not* allocate funds to States.

chapters.heading: 5. Balance of Payments, Foreign Trade & International Institutions
chapters.body_markdown:
**Core Mental Model:** **Balance of Payments (BoP)** records all economic transactions between a country and the rest of the world in two accounts: **Current Account** (trade in goods/services + remittances) and **Capital Account** (FDI, FPI, external borrowings).

### Current Account vs. Capital Account

| BoP Account | What Goes Inside |
| --- | --- |
| **Current Account** | Export & import of **goods** (Balance of Trade), **services** (IT, tourism), primary income (dividends/interest), **remittances & unilateral transfers** |
| **Capital / Financial Account** | **FDI** (long-term ownership/management ≥10%), **FPI/FII** (portfolio stocks/bonds), External Commercial Borrowings (ECB), NRI deposits |

### Key Global Economic Institutions

| Institution | HQ | Core Mandate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **IMF** (Bretton Woods, 1944) | Washington D.C. | BoP crisis lending, exchange stability, **SDR** (Special Drawing Rights) |
| **World Bank** (IBRD + IDA) | Washington D.C. | Long-term development & poverty reduction loans |
| **WTO** (1995, replaced GATT) | Geneva | Global trade rules, tariff reduction, dispute settlement |
| **ADB** (1966) / **NDB** (BRICS) | Manila / Shanghai | Asian & BRICS infrastructure/development finance |

**Exam Trap:** **Balance of Trade (BoT)** counts **only visible goods** (merchandise); **Current Account** counts goods + invisible services + remittances. **Devaluation** (official fixed-rate cut) or **Depreciation** (market fall) makes **exports cheaper** and **imports costlier**.

title: Reasoning & Mental Ability
summary: 6 shortcut-packed Reasoning chapters — EJOTY Series, Coding-Decoding, Circular/Linear Seating, Blood Relations & Directions, Clocks/Calendars/Mirror-Water Images, and Data Interpretation — linked to 1,533+ Reasoning PYQs.

chapters.heading: 1. Number, Alphabet & Alphanumeric Series (EJOTY Trick)
chapters.body_markdown:
**Core Mental Model:** Every series follows one of six disciplined engines — check **differences first**, then **double differences**, then **alternating series**, then **squares/cubes (n² ± 1, n³ ± 1)**, then **multipliers**, and for letters convert to numbers using **EJOTY**.

### Alphabet Position Shortcuts (A=1 … Z=26)

| Anchor Letter | Position | Opposite Pair (Sum = 27) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **E** | 5 | E ↔ V (5 + 22 = 27) |
| **J** | 10 | J ↔ Q (10 + 17 = 27) |
| **O** | 15 | O ↔ L (15 + 12 = 27) |
| **T** | 20 | T ↔ G (20 + 7 = 27) |
| **Y** | 25 | Y ↔ B (25 + 2 = 27) |

**Worked Example:** *MPSC Series:* `SCD, TEF, UGH, ____, WKL`. Split each triplet into 3 independent tracks: 1st letters `S → T → U → V → W` (+1); 2nd & 3rd letters `CD → EF → GH → IJ → KL` (+2 pairs). Answer = **`VIJ`**.

**Exam Trap:** If a number series jumps up and down unpredictably (e.g., `2, 15, 4, 12, 6, 9, ?`), immediately split into **two interleaved alternating series** (odd positions vs even positions).

chapters.heading: 2. Coding-Decoding, Analogy & Odd-One-Out
chapters.body_markdown:
**Core Mental Model:** Write the original word **directly above** the coded word and inspect column-by-column: check (1) uniform shift (`+k` / `-k`), (2) **reverse order** + shift, (3) **opposite letters** (sum = 27), (4) **case / vowel–consonant** rules, and (5) **direct substitution**.

**Worked Example:** *MPSC Coding:* `POTASSIUM` is coded as `PoTassium` — how is `GRAPHITE` coded? Notice the exact pattern: letters at positions 1 and 3 stay **UPPERCASE**, all other letters become **lowercase** (`P` o `T` assium → `G` r `A` phite = **`GrAphite`**). Always inspect capitalisation and letter swaps before hunting for arithmetic shifts!

- **Analogy checklist:** Capital–Country, Instrument–Measurement, Worker–Tool, Animal–Young One, Cause–Effect, Synonym/Antonym, `n : n² + n`.
- **Odd-One-Out priority:** Prime numbers → Squares/Cubes → Divisibility → Digit sum → Vowel count.

**Memory Hook:** Opposite-letter pairs (sum = 27): **A**Z (Azad), **B**Y (Boy), **C**X (Crux), **D**W (Dew), **E**V (Even), **F**U (Full), **G**T (GT Road), **H**S (High School), **I**R (Indian Railway), **J**Q (Jungle Queen), **K**P (Kanpur), **L**O (Love), **M**N (Man).

chapters.heading: 3. Seating Arrangements (Circular & Linear) & Ranking
chapters.body_markdown:
**Core Mental Model:** Never guess seating layouts in your head — draw slots immediately and anchor the **most constrained clue first** (e.g., “second to the left of X” or “not at any end”).

### Circular & Ranking Formulas

| Situation | Rule / Formula |
| --- | --- |
| Facing **Centre** (Circle) | **Left = Clockwise**; **Right = Anti-clockwise** |
| Facing **Outside** (Circle) | **Left = Anti-clockwise**; **Right = Clockwise** |
| Facing **North** (Row) | Left = your left; Right = your right (Facing South = flipped!) |
| Total in a Row (Rank from both ends) | `Total = Left Rank + Right Rank − 1` |
| People strictly between A and B (non-overlap) | `Between = Total − (Left_A + Right_B)` |
| Position swap between two people | `Total = New_Pos(A) + Old_Pos(B) − 1` |

**Worked Example:** *Ranking:* If Ram is 12th from the left and 19th from the right in a queue, total students = `12 + 19 − 1 = 30`. Always subtract 1 so Ram is not counted twice.

**Exam Trap:** In phrasing like *“A sits 2nd to the right of B, **who** sits next to C”*, the pronoun **“who / whom / whose”** refers to the **immediately preceding person (B)**, whereas **“and / but”** refers to the **first subject (A)**.

chapters.heading: 4. Blood Relations & Direction Sense
chapters.body_markdown:
**Core Mental Model:** Draw a **3-row family tree** (vertical lines = parent/child, double horizontal `=` = married couple, single horizontal `—` = siblings, `+` male / `−` female). For Directions, track **Net North–South** and **Net East–West** separately, then apply Pythagoras.

### Direction & Shadow Shortcuts

| Case | Fast Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Shortest distance | `√(ΔN-S² + ΔE-W²)` — watch for **3–4–5**, **5–12–13**, **8–15–17** triples! |
| Turn cancellation | Every `1 Left + 1 Right` cancels out; `4 Right` or `4 Left` = same direction; `2 Right` = opposite |
| **Morning** (Sun in East) | Shadows fall **West**. If shadow is to your **Left**, you face **North** |
| **Evening** (Sun in West) | Shadows fall **East**. If shadow is to your **Left**, you face **South** |

**Exam Trap:** In Blood Relations, **never assume gender from a name** (e.g., “Kiran” or “Zira”) unless explicitly stated via *son, daughter, father, sister, husband, wife*. Break pointing questions backwards starting from **“my …”**.

chapters.heading: 5. Syllogisms, Venn Diagrams, Clocks, Calendars & Mirror/Water Images
chapters.body_markdown:
**Core Mental Model:** Turn visual & time puzzles into **exact mechanical formulas** so you never second-guess under exam pressure.

### Clocks, Calendars & Mirror/Water Image Formulas

| Topic | Exact Formula / Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Angle between Clock Hands at `H : M` | `θ = |30H − 5.5M|` (reflex angle = `360° − θ`) |
| Hands coincide / opposite / right-angle | In 12 hrs: **11** times coincide, **11** times opposite (180°), **22** times right-angle (90°) |
| Calendar Odd Days | Normal year (365d) = **1 odd day**; Leap year (366d) = **2 odd days**; 100/200/300/400 yrs = **5 / 3 / 1 / 0** |
| **Mirror Image** (Vertical mirror) | **Left ↔ Right flips**; Top & Bottom stay unchanged |
| **Water Image** (Horizontal mirror) | **Top ↔ Bottom flips**; Left & Right stay unchanged |
| Syllogism “Either–Or” | Both conclusions individually false + same subject/predicate + complementary pair (*Some + No* or *Some + Some not*) |

**Worked Example:** *Clock Angle at 3:20:* `θ = |30(3) − 5.5(20)| = |90 − 110| = 20°`.

**Exam Trap:** Century years (`1900`, `2100`) are **NOT leap years** unless divisible by **400** (`2000`, `2400` are leap years). In Syllogisms, a definite conclusion must hold in **all** valid Venn diagrams — never assume “Some A are B” implies “Some A are not B”.

chapters.heading: 6. Data Interpretation & Analytical Decision-Making
chapters.body_markdown:
**Core Mental Model:** 90% of Data Interpretation (Tables, Bar Graphs, Line Charts, Pie Charts) uses just **three calculations**: Percentage Change, Ratio, and Average — speed comes from **approximation & fraction equivalents**.

### Pie Chart & DI Speed Conversions

| Quantity | Conversion |
| --- | --- |
| Pie Chart Full Circle | `100% = 360°` → `1% = 3.6°` and `10% = 36°` |
| % More / Less than B | `(Difference ÷ Base after “than”) × 100` |
| Growth Rate (CAGR approx.) | Check absolute jump vs smaller base year first |
| Decision-Making / Conflict Resolution | Pick options that are **objective, lawful, evidence-based, and collaborative** — reject extreme, biased, or impulsive choices |

**Exam Trap:** In Pie Charts, never compute raw values for two slices if the question only asks for their **ratio** or **percentage difference** — divide the **percentages or central angles directly** to save 45 seconds!
